name: NRF5340-QKAA-R7
title: nRF5340 dual Arm Cortex-M33 Bluetooth 5.2, IEEE 802.15.4 and 2.4 GHz SoC, 128 MHz + 64 MHz, 1 MB + 256 kB flash, 512 kB + 64 kB RAM, USB, NFC
summary: A multiprotocol 2.4 GHz system-on-chip with two Arm Cortex-M33 cores: an application core at up to 128 MHz with FPU, DSP and TrustZone, 1 MB of flash and 512 kB of RAM, and a 64 MHz network core with 256 kB of flash and 64 kB of RAM that runs the radio for Bluetooth LE 5.2, IEEE 802.15.4, ANT and proprietary protocols. It carries CryptoCell-312, QSPI with execute-in-place, USB, NFC-A, SPI, I2C, UART, I2S, PDM, PWM and a 12-bit 200 ksps ADC, runs from 1.7 V to 5.5 V on VDD or VDDH, and works from -40 °C to 105 °C. NRF5340-QKAA-R7 is the aQFN94 7 x 7 mm part on a 7-inch reel.

Its peripherals: SPI master/slave, I2C-compatible two-wire master/slave and UART with CTS/RTS, all with EasyDMA; three 32-bit timers with counter mode; two RTCs; a temperature sensor; DPPI; IPC and MUTEX.

Bluetooth 5.2, IEEE 802.15.4-2006 and 2.4 GHz transceiver. Sensitivity -98 dBm at 1 Mbps BLE, -104 dBm at 125 kbps BLE long range, -101 dBm in IEEE 802.15.4. TX power -40 dBm to +3 dBm. Data rates: Bluetooth 5.2 at 2 Mbps, 1 Mbps, 500 kbps and 125 kbps; IEEE 802.15.4-2006 at 250 kbps; proprietary 2.4 GHz at 2 Mbps and 1 Mbps. Angle-of-arrival and angle-of-departure direction finding over BLE. Single-ended antenna output with the balun on chip. 128-bit AES/ECB/CCM/AAR co-processor encrypts packets on the fly. 3.2 mA in TX at 0 dBm, 2.6 mA in RX. RSSI with 1 dB resolution. Works over the air with nRF52, nRF51, nRF24L and nRF24AP series devices.

Arm TrustZone CryptoCell-312: random number generator compliant with NIST 800-90B, AIS-31 and FIPS 140-2; AES-128 and AES-256 in the modes ECB, CBC, CTR, GCM, CCM/CCM* and CMAC/CBC-MAC; SHA-1 and SHA-2 up to 256 bits; HMAC; RSA up to 3072-bit keys; ECC on the common curves; application keys managed by a derived-key model.

QSPI for external flash, with execute-in-place and optional on-the-fly encryption and decryption. NFC-A tag that can wake the chip when a field appears and supports touch-to-pair. Up to five SPI master/slave, up to four I2C-compatible two-wire master/slave and up to four UART (CTS/RTS) instances, all with EasyDMA. I2S and PDM audio interfaces. Four PWM units with EasyDMA. A 12-bit, 200 ksps ADC, also with EasyDMA, has eight channels, each configurable and with programmable gain. Three 32-bit timers that can also count events, two 24-bit RTCs, two quadrature decoders, DPPI, IPC and MUTEX.
aQFN94, 7 x 7 mm, and WLCSP95, 4.4 x 4.0 mm.

Computer peripherals and I/O devices such as multi-touch trackpads; wearables for health and fitness and for wireless payment; wireless audio including Bluetooth LE Audio, true wireless earbuds, headphones, microphones and speakers; IoT sensors and controllers for the smart home and industry; interactive entertainment such as remote controls and gaming controllers; professional and connected lighting.

Each peripheral has a short upper-case name, such as TIMER, used in headings and in the CMSIS hardware abstraction layer. An instance adds a number from 0, such as TIMER0, when the peripheral exists more than once; CMSIS uses the instance name too. Electrical specifications of peripherals hold over the recommended operating conditions.

A blank field in a register is reserved: it reads as undefined and must be written as 0. Hexadecimal values carry a 0x prefix; decimal values have none. A value range [a..b] includes both ends. A field marked Deprecated is not for new designs.

nRF5340 is a 2.4 GHz multiprotocol system-on-chip with two Arm Cortex-M33 processors. Its radio handles Bluetooth Low Energy and ANT, plus IEEE 802.15.4 as used by Thread and Zigbee, and proprietary 2.4 GHz protocols can be built on it. The application core has DSP instructions and an FPU, runs at up to 128 MHz (or 64 MHz to save energy) with 1 MB flash and 512 kB RAM. The network core is a cut-down Cortex-M33 for low power at a fixed 64 MHz with 256 kB of flash and 64 kB of RAM. Both share the power, clock and peripheral architecture of the nRF51, nRF52 and nRF91 series. Security comes from Arm TrustZone, Arm CryptoCell-312 and blocks for system protection and key management.

Every memory and register of both cores lies in one address space. The application core's two 256 kB RAM blocks appear as one contiguous 512 kB block; the first has single-cycle CPU access and the second adds up to four CPU cycles of latency. The application core's memory is mapped into the network core's map, so the network CPU can share data with the application through it; the application core can limit this through the DCNF PROTECT registers, and when the network core is marked non-secure under TrustZone it cannot reach secure memory or peripherals set by the SPU. EasyDMA masters of network-core peripherals cannot reach application-core RAM, and the network CPU cannot run code from application-core flash or reach QSPI XIP memory.

RAM has no limit on reads or writes. Each RAM AHB slave of a core connects to one or more RAM sections, and every section's power can be controlled on its own in System ON and in System OFF; the VMC manages them.

Flash can be read without limit but has a limited number of write and erase cycles and restrictions on how it is written. The NVMC handles writes. The application core's flash is in 4 kB pages, the network core's in 2 kB pages.
The application core can run code straight from an external flash device over the QSPI, and that flash can be encrypted and decrypted on the fly.
Reaching memory or peripherals across a bus bridge adds latency, for example when the network core reads application-core memory or peripherals.

A power management unit (PMU) watches which clocks and supplies the two cores and their peripherals need at each moment, and starts or stops clock sources and picks regulator modes on its own to keep current low. It takes power from VDD or VDDH, a 32 MHz crystal and an optional 32.768 kHz crystal, and feeds both cores.

System ON is the mode after a power-on reset. The CPUs and peripherals idle or run as software directs; the network core can also sit in Force-OFF. Internal voltages scale with demand: a higher internal voltage, and so more current, is drawn when the application core clock is 128 MHz (also while its CPU sleeps in WFI or WFE, so dropping to 64 MHz before sleep saves current), when QSPI runs at 96 MHz, when USB is in use, while debugging, and when extra voltage is requested on VREGRADIO through VREQCTRL.

With every CPU and peripheral idle, System ON rests in one of two submodes. Constant latency keeps a set of resources on so that CPU wakeup and PPI task response are short and fixed, at the price of more current; the CONSTLAT task selects it. Low-power lets the automatic power management choose the most frugal supply, so wakeup and task response times vary; the LOWPWR task selects it, and it is the default on entering System ON. Each core has its own POWER peripheral; a Constant latency request from either one wins over Low-power.

System OFF is the deepest saving mode: core functions lose power and all running tasks end. It is entered through the SYSTEMOFF register. Wakeup sources: the GPIO DETECT signal, the LPCOMP ANADETECT signal, the NFCT SENSE signal (wake on field), a valid voltage on VBUS, the start of a debug session, and a pin reset. Waking performs a system reset. RAM sections can be kept through System OFF by the retention settings in VMC. EasyDMA transfers should be finished first (no EasyDMA peripheral active), and the network core should be idle.

In Debug Interface mode System OFF is only emulated, so the debug resources (CLOCK, POWER, OSCILLATORS, REGULATORS, RESET, NVMC, the CPU, flash and RAM) stay available. The CPU keeps running in this case, so an endless loop placed right after the System OFF entry keeps it from running code meant never to execute.

Force-OFF applies to the network core only. The application core puts it there through the RESET register interface (NETWORK.FORCEOFF), stopping it for the lowest current, and only the application core can release it; the network core then wakes with a reset and its CPU starts again. Before forcing it off, the network core should be idle: peripherals stopped, any extra VREGRADIO voltage request cancelled in VREQCTRL, and its CPU in WFI or WFE. RAM sections can be retained through Force-OFF by the VMC settings. In Debug Interface mode Force-OFF is emulated: the CPU and peripherals are reset, and the CPU is kept from running while a debugger reaches that core's RAM, flash or peripherals.

Since the PMU keeps adjusting supplies and clocks, typical currents from VDD or VDDH are given as a set of scenarios, each a list of operations and conditions. A common set of conditions applies to every scenario unless the scenario states otherwise.

Two supply ranges each have their own pin, and the PMU turns on the right regulator for whichever pin carries the supply. Three regulators serve the chip: VREGH (high voltage, VDDH to VDD), VREGMAIN (from VDD, powers the application core) and VREGRADIO (from VDD, powers the network core and radio). A fourth, USBREG, serves only USB from VBUS and is controlled on its own.

VDD and VDDH are tied together and both take the external supply (1.7 V to 3.6 V); VREGH switches itself off and only VREGMAIN and VREGRADIO work. VDDH must be joined to VDD even though VREGH is unused. Both regulators start in LDO mode; DC/DC mode is turned on for each separately (VREGMAIN.DCDCEN, VREGRADIO.DCDCEN). Each regulator in DC/DC mode needs its external LC filter: an inductor from DCCD to DECD for VREGMAIN and from DCC to DECR for VREGRADIO, with decoupling CVDD on VDD and CDECD, CDECR on DECD, DECR. A regulator kept in LDO mode needs no inductor. DC/DC mode draws less current overall; its efficiency depends on supply voltage and load.

The supply (2.5 V to 5.5 V) goes to VDDH only. VREGH makes VDD, and VREGMAIN and VREGRADIO run from VDD. All three start in LDO mode and each can be switched to DC/DC (VREGMAIN.DCDCEN, VREGH.DCDCEN, VREGRADIO.DCDCEN); VREGH in DC/DC mode needs an inductor from DCCH to VDD, with CVDDH on VDDH and CVDD on VDD. VREGH output on VDD can power external circuits in System ON and System OFF; its voltage, 1.8 V to 3.3 V, is set in UICR.VREGHVOUT, and VDDH has to exceed it by VREGH,DROP. Out of reset VREGH is set up to source external parts from VDD; turning that off saves power. The external current allowed depends on how much the chip itself draws (IEXT limits). MAINREGSTATUS.VREGH reads 1 in high voltage mode and 0 in normal voltage mode.

A supply mode detector decides at power-up which supply pin is in use, sets the supply mode, enables VREGH when needed and issues the power-on reset. A brownout detector watches VDD (the VREGMAIN input) and holds the chip in brownout reset while VDD is below VBOR (VBOR,OFF in System OFF, VBOR,ON in System ON).

The optional power-fail comparator (POF), set up and enabled in POFCON, warns of a falling supply without resetting: when the supply drops below the threshold it sends the POFWARN event to the POWER peripheral of both cores, giving software time for an orderly shutdown. VPOF (VDD, normal voltage mode) is set from 1.7 V to 2.8 V and VPOFH (VDDH, high voltage mode) from 2.7 V to 4.2 V, both in 100 mV steps, with VPOFHYST of hysteresis. POFWARN also fires if the supply is already below the threshold when the POF is enabled or the threshold is raised above it. While enabled with the supply below threshold, the POF blocks NVMC writes to non-volatile memory. It is inactive in System OFF and in System ON while HFCLK is stopped.

Each core's POWER peripheral is its interface to the power and clock system for tasks, events and interrupts (CONSTLAT, LOWPWR, POFWARN, SLEEPENTER, SLEEPEXIT). It shares its interrupt enable registers with CLOCK and holds two retained general-purpose registers, GPREGRET[0..1]. RAM block power is handled by VMC.
The GPIO high level follows the supply mode: the voltage on VDD in normal voltage mode, and the VREGHVOUT setting in high voltage mode.

USB signalling (D+, D- and the D+ pull-up) runs from a dedicated regulator that turns the 5 V on VBUS into 3.3 V on DECUSB; the rest of USBD runs from the main supply, so USB needs VBUS and the VDD/VDDH supply both. VBUS entering its valid range gives the USBDETECTED event and leaving it gives USBREMOVED; VBUS arriving in System OFF resets the chip into System ON with the VBUS bit set in RESETREAS. With USBD enabled and VBUS present the regulator turns on, and USBPWRRDY follows once its worst-case settling time has passed, after which the D+ pull-up may be enabled. USBREGSTATUS reports VBUS detection and output readiness at any time. VBUS and DECUSB each need a decoupling capacitor (CVBUS, CDECUSB) for stability.

VREQCTRL, in the network core, raises the VREGRADIO supply so the radio can transmit at +3 dBm. Setting VREGRADIO.VREQH requests the higher voltage and holds the request until cleared; VREGRADIO.VREQHREADY reads Ready once the regulator has switched, and software waits for it before relying on the higher voltage.

Resets are system-level (power-on, brownout, pin reset; all cores) or core-level (soft reset, CPU lockup, watchdog; the whole core or part of it). Other sources are wakeup from System OFF (from GPIO, NFC, LPCOMP or VBUS), a soft reset through each core's CTRL-AP over SWD, and NETWORK.FORCEOFF. After a system reset the application core starts by itself and the network core stays held until the application core releases it. Each core has a RESETREAS register naming the source; the network core's copy also shows system-level and application core sources unless stated.

Power-on reset keeps the chip in reset until VDD (made by VREGH in high voltage mode) is at least the minimum operating voltage and the on-chip regulators have started. A pin reset comes from asserting the RESET pin, whose internal pull-up equals a GPIO pull-up. Brownout reset holds the chip while VDD is under the brownout threshold. After each of these, and after wakeup from System OFF, the application core runs and the network core is kept in reset. A wakeup from System OFF leaves the DAP untouched while the chip is in Debug Interface mode.

Setting SYSRESETREQ in the Arm AIRCR register gives a soft reset; the CTRL-AP RESET register can do the same. A soft reset or a watchdog reset of the application core also holds the network core in reset; in the network core either one resets only that core. Each core has its own WDT, so the application core does not learn of a network core watchdog timeout unless told, for example by the network core reading its RESETREAS WDT flags and reporting over IPC.

NETWORK.FORCEOFF in the application core holds the network core off (its reset value is Hold). Any application core reset puts the network core in Force-OFF, seen there as the FORCEOFF reset source, until the application core releases it. Retained registers keep their value through System OFF, Force-OFF and some resets, by source. RAM is never cleared by a reset, but its contents may be corrupted depending on the source. In System OFF and Force-OFF the watchdog does not run and no CPU lockup can occur; in Debug Interface mode debug blocks are not reset and a CPU lockup causes no reset.

Each core has its own clock control, which asks the shared power and clock system for clocks and hands them to its CPU and peripherals; branches nobody uses are gated off. Sources are the internal 192, 128 and 64 MHz oscillators (HFINT), the 32 MHz crystal oscillator (HFXO, with optional internal load capacitors), the audio oscillator, the 32.768 kHz RC oscillator (LFRC, with calibration), the 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator (LFXO) and a 32.768 kHz clock synthesised from HFCLK (LFSYNT). Switching between sources is glitch-free. The network core clock control has no HFCLKAUDIO or HFCLK192M, and its HFCLKCTRL resets to 0x0. CLOCK shares its interrupt enable registers with POWER.

CPUs and peripherals request high-frequency clocks from their core's HFCLK control automatically; when requests from every core stop (CPU asleep, peripherals done) the clock stops. HFCLK clocks exist only in System ON, and an automatic request is served by HFINT, which stops again when no longer wanted. The HFCLKSTART task starts the source chosen in HFCLKSRC for HFCLK128M/HFCLK64M, HFCLK192MSTART the one in HFCLK192MSRC, and HFCLKAUDIOSTART always starts HFXO; each gives its STARTED event once the oscillator runs at a stable frequency. Source registers may be written at any time but take effect only at the next START. Repeated START tasks before STARTED give one STARTED event. Every core that triggered a START must also trigger the matching STOP before the source stops. Keeping a source running ahead of need shortens start-up at the cost of current.

HFXO has to be selected and started for the RADIO (network HFCLKSTART), for USBD to answer USB traffic (application HFCLK192MSTART), to put NFCT in the activated state (application HFCLKSTART) and to cut SAADC clock jitter (application HFCLKSTART). Its start-up time is the HFXO power-up time plus the count time set in HFXOCNT, so crystals with different start-up behaviour can be used. Core clocks sharing one HFCLK clock share its source, so a block that did not ask for HFXO may still get the more accurate clock.

HCLK128M is divided from HFCLK128M through HFCLKCTRL, and the 192 MHz QSPI clock from HFCLK192M through HFCLK192MCTRL (divide by 1, 2 or 4; reset value divide by 4), at any time, even while running. The Div1 and Div2 settings of HFCLK192MCTRL raise current consumption. ACLK is not divided; its frequency is set in the peripherals that use it.

The audio oscillator gives a low-jitter clock, always from HFXO, tunable in 3.3 ppm steps over two bands, 11.176 to 11.402 MHz and 12.165 to 12.411 MHz, for I2S and PDM, which select it in their own configuration. HFCLKAUDIOSTART must be triggered before use; after HFCLKAUDIOSTOP it keeps running while a peripheral still uses it. The frequency is set in HFCLKAUDIO.FREQUENCY and can be trimmed to follow audio arriving from an asynchronous source. Peripherals must be stopped when changing between the two bands.

The automatic control can be overridden so a clock stays on with no request, avoiding start-up time and keeping full accuracy after sleep: choose the source in HFCLKSRC (or HFCLK192MSRC), set ALWAYSRUN in HFCLKALWAYSRUN (or HFCLK192MALWAYSRUN), then trigger HFCLKSTART (or HFCLK192MSTART). For the audio clock, set HFCLKAUDIOALWAYSRUN.ALWAYSRUN and trigger HFCLKAUDIOSTART; its source is always HFXO. These registers can be written at any time and act only at the START task.

Each core's LFCLK control delivers the 32.768 kHz PCLK32KI clock. Sources are LFRC (the default), LFXO and LFSYNT; all are off in System OFF. Peripherals such as RTC and WDT request it automatically, and such requests always use LFRC unless LFCLKSTART has been triggered, in which case the source is the LFCLKSRC value at that last trigger. LFCLKSTARTED follows once the source runs; repeated starts before it give one event. The clock stops when nothing requests it and LFCLKSTOP has been triggered in every core that started it. With LFXO chosen, the clock first runs from LFRC and moves to LFXO once the crystal is running. If two cores request different sources the most accurate one runs; one cycle may be lost when the source changes. The same ALWAYSRUN override exists through LFCLKALWAYSRUN: set LFCLKSRC.SRC, set ALWAYSRUN, trigger LFCLKSTART.

LFRC needs no external parts. Its accuracy improves by calibrating against HFXO while it runs: the CAL task requests HFCLK from HFXO for the duration and DONE marks the end. CAL during a running calibration has no effect; each core may trigger CAL and each gets its own DONE. A core changing the LFCLK source aborts calibration, and the core that triggered CAL then gets no DONE.

LFXO, with an external crystal on XL1 and XL2, is required when the LFCLK has to be better than ±250 ppm. LFSYNT derives the 32.768 kHz clock from HFCLK and inherits its accuracy (HFXO for high accuracy); it saves the 32.768 kHz crystal but raises average current because HFCLK must keep running.

The oscillators are shared by both cores and run under the clock control. HFXO takes a 32 MHz AT-cut crystal in parallel resonance between XC1 and XC2, with a ceramic capacitor (C1, C2, equal values) from each pin to ground, chosen so that the total load the crystal sees, including PCB stray capacitance (Cpcb1, Cpcb2) and pin capacitance (Cpin), matches the crystal's specified load capacitance. The crystal's load capacitance, shunt capacitance, ESR and drive level must stay within the HFXO limits; a crystal below the maximum load and shunt capacitance starts faster and draws less current.

XC1 and XC2 have optional internal load capacitors from 7.0 pF to 20.0 pF in 0.5 pF steps that replace C1 and C2. They must be set before HFXO starts: compute XOSC32MCAPS.CAPVALUE from the wanted capacitance and the factory trim values in FICR XOSC32MTRIM (SLOPE, a two's-complement value from -16 to 15, and OFFSET, 0 to 31), then set XOSC32MCAPS.ENABLE. Precomputing (CAPACITANCE × 2 − 14) avoids floating point.

A 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XL1 and XL2 (P0.00 and P0.01), whose PIN_CNF MCUSEL field must be set to Peripheral. Equal ceramic capacitors C1 and C2 go from each pin to ground and set the load capacitance with the stray and pin capacitance. Instead, an internal capacitor of 6, 7 or 9 pF between XL1 and XL2 (XOSC32KI.INTCAP) can replace the external ones; it is the capacitance across the crystal including pin capacitance but not PCB stray, and must match the crystal's load capacitance.

LFXO also accepts an external 32.768 kHz clock with LFCLKSRC.SRC = LFXO: a low-swing clock on XL1 with XL2 grounded and XOSC32KI.BYPASS = Disabled, or a rail-to-rail clock on XL1 with XL2 unconnected and XOSC32KI.BYPASS = Enabled.

The application core is a microcontroller with on-chip flash and an Arm Cortex-M33 with DSP instructions (single-cycle MAC, hardware divide, 8- and 16-bit SIMD), a single-precision FPU, an MPU and TrustZone for Armv8-M; CMSIS is available. Around it sit serial, analog and cryptographic peripherals. NVIC handles prioritised events with deterministic timing. Code from internal or external flash runs with wait states, which the instruction cache reduces. FPU exceptions can raise interrupts through the FPU peripheral.

The CPU (through an 8 kB two-way set-associative cache on its code bus), the network core and the EasyDMA peripherals reach memory through the AHB multilayer interconnect. Flash (CODE0) holds 256 pages of 4 kB from 0x0000 0000 (page 255 at 0x000F F000); external QSPI memory appears read-only (XIP) from 0x1000 0000; RAM0 to RAM7, each with 16 sections, start at 0x2000 0000, 0x2001 0000 and so on to 0x2007 0000. DCNF registers can block access from external masters (EXTPERI, EXTRAM, EXTCODE ports).

The application core cache is two-way set associative with least-recently-used replacement and 128-bit lines, and caches instruction and data reads over the code bus from internal flash and the XIP region. It can serve as a cache or as general-purpose RAM (MODE = Ram; switching to Ram clears it, switching back invalidates it). Its contents (data, tag, valid and MRU bits) are mapped read-only at CACHEDATA (0x00F00000) and CACHEINFO (0x00F08000) for profiling; DEBUGLOCK can block that view, and WRITELOCK stops misses from replacing lines while lookups continue. Invalidation, erase, disabling, and hit/miss counters per region (flash, XIP) for instructions and data (IHIT, IMISS, DHIT, DMISS; enabled in PROFILINGENABLE, cleared together by PROFILINGCLEAR) are provided.

FICR at 0x00FF0000 holds factory-programmed, unerasable chip data: configuration and device IDs, part, variant, package, RAM and flash size, code page size, NFC tag header defaults, TRNG 90B parameters and the XOSC32MTRIM trims. UICR at 0x00FF8000 is non-volatile user configuration, including VREGHVOUT, and from offset 0x100 up holds cryptographic key slots handled by the KMU (128 slots, each four 32-bit words; a revoked slot cannot be restored). Neither is reachable from the network core.

The AHB multilayer gives masters parallel paths to slaves. When masters want the same slave, the higher priority goes first; a lower one waits until the higher pauses or finishes, and is stalled after its current word if a higher one arrives. Masters of equal priority exclude each other. Some masters, such as I2S (and RADIO in the network core), cannot stall safely and may lose data under contention, so either keep masters off a shared slave or keep the bandwidth from running out.

The network core is a microcontroller with its own flash and an Arm Cortex-M33 (hardware divide, 8- and 16-bit SIMD, MPU; no FPU, DSP extension or TrustZone), with the peripherals for Bluetooth LE, IEEE 802.15.4 and proprietary 2.4 GHz protocols: RADIO, RNG, TEMP, ACL, ECB, CCM and AAR, plus its own timers, RTCs, serial interface, GPIOTE, DPPI, IPC, EGU, WDT, CLOCK, POWER and VMC. Flash wait states are reduced by its cache.

Network core flash (CODE0, with a 2 kB direct-mapped cache) has 128 pages of 2 kB from 0x0100 0000 (page 127 at 0x0103 F800). RAM0 to RAM3, four sections each, start at 0x2100 0000, 0x2100 4000, 0x2100 8000 and 0x2100 C000. The network core can reach application core flash, RAM and peripherals when the application core's DCNF and SPU allow it; a small part of application RAM is set aside for messages between the cores. Network core peripherals cannot be reached from the application core.

The network core has its own FICR at 0x01FF0000 (device IDs and sizes, encryption root ER and identity root IR, device address type and device address, trim data) and its own UICR at 0x01FF8000 (APPROTECT, ERASEPROTECT, words reserved for Nordic firmware and words for the customer).

Each core has its own peripherals; application core peripherals can be reached from the network core but not the reverse. Peripherals are run through configuration, task and event registers. Each owns a 0x1000-byte block of address space, and its ID follows from the base address (0x40000000 is ID 0, 0x40001000 ID 1, 0x4001F000 ID 31); its single interrupt line has the same number in the NVIC. Peripherals sharing an ID (except ID 0) share resources and only one may be enabled at a time; to switch, disable the old one, remove its DPPI connections, write INTENCLR = 0xFFFFFFFF, configure the new one fully and then enable it.

Configuration registers are written before the peripheral is enabled, and tasks and events work only once it is enabled. PSEL pin selections take effect only when written while disabled; a new PSEL connects four CPU cycles after the write. Most registers are lost in System OFF and on reset; retained ones are marked. Registers with many single-bit fields may have SET and CLR companions at the next two addresses: writing 1 sets or clears that bit, writing 0 does nothing, and reading either returns the main register.

A task starts when firmware writes 1 to it or a peripheral signal toggles it. An event register is set when the peripheral raises the event and cleared by writing 0; events can recur while it still reads 1. Events can be published and tasks subscribed on DPPI channels through PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE registers. Shortcuts are fixed event-to-task links inside one peripheral, up to 32, each enabled by one bit in SHORTS, with less delay than DPPI. Any event can drive the interrupt through INTEN, INTENSET and INTENCLR (some peripherals have only the last two). An interrupt is cleared by writing 0 to its event register; read the register back before leaving the handler so the clear has landed, and likewise read INTEN or INTENCLR after disabling an interrupt in a handler.

To move a peripheral between secure and non-secure in the SPU: stop it, disable it, disconnect its pins and DPPI links, return sensitive registers to their defaults, change the SPU setting, then enable it again.

EasyDMA is an AHB master inside some peripherals that reads and writes Data RAM directly; it cannot reach flash. A peripheral may have several channels, for example a READER and a WRITER, each set by a PTR (start address) and a MAXCNT (buffer size; never larger than the buffer). After a transfer AMOUNT holds the bytes moved. PTR must point to valid RAM before use (its reset value may not); a pointer outside RAM can cause a HardFault or RAM corruption. Under bus contention a peripheral either stalls or loses data, depending on the peripheral. Channels with a LIST register support array list mode, where consecutive MAXCNT-sized buffers follow one another in RAM.

ACL, in the network core, applies access permissions to regions of the network core's own flash. Each of eight entries has ADDR (word-aligned start on a flash page boundary), SIZE (whole flash pages, at most the flash size) and PERM (read and write bits). Protection starts two CPU cycles after all three are written, and only with a valid page-aligned ADDR and non-zero SIZE and PERM. Each register can be written once and is cleared only by a reset, so the boot code sets them. A violation is blocked and raises a BusFault; a debugger reads protected regions as zero and its writes are ignored.

AAR resolves Bluetooth resolvable private addresses in real time, so incoming packets can be filtered against a list of shared Identity Resolving Keys; generating such addresses is done with ECB instead. A resolvable address is six bytes: a 24-bit hash and a 24-bit prand whose top two bits are 1 then 0. ADDRPTR points at the packet start, IRKPTR at a list of up to 16 IRKs of 16 bytes each, NIRK sets how many are tried, and SCRATCHPTR at a scratch area of at least 3 bytes, all in Data RAM. START begins; RESOLVED or NOTRESOLVED reports the result and END follows when it stops. The address type is not checked. AAR can start as soon as RADIO has stored the six address bytes. Resolution time depends on where the matching key sits in the list and on RAM traffic. AAR, CCM and ECB share one AES core, ECB having the lowest priority, and AAR shares ID 14 with CCM.

CCM is AES-128 counter mode with CBC-MAC, meeting the Bluetooth LE requirements (IETF RFC 3610, NIST SP 800-38C). It generates a keystream (KSGEN, ending with ENDKSGEN), then encrypts or decrypts a packet (CRYPT, ending with ENDCRYPT), with an optional shortcut from ENDKSGEN to CRYPT. Its settings come from MODE and the data structure at CNFPTR (key, packet counter, direction bit, IV), from which hardware builds the nonce; the keystream sits in the scratch area at SCRATCHPTR. Keystream length is 27 bytes for default-length packets, or MAXPACKETSIZE for extended length, up to 251 bytes, which caps the payload at 251 bytes. With the shortcut in use INPTR and OUTPTR must be set before KSGEN.

Encrypting reads the plain packet at INPTR, encrypts it, appends a 4-byte MIC, adds 4 to the length field and writes the result to OUTPTR. Decrypting reads at INPTR, decrypts, checks the MIC (header S0 included, masked by HEADERMASK), subtracts 4 from the length and writes to OUTPTR, with the result in MICSTATUS. Payloads must be at least 5 bytes (one byte or more of data plus the MIC), so lengths 1 to 4 give a MIC error. Empty packets (length 0) pass through untouched and always pass the MIC check. The length field width is set in MODE.

CCM can work on the fly with RADIO when the MODE data rate matches the radio's; RATEOVERRIDE can change it during a packet. When transmitting, CCM OUTPTR and RADIO PACKETPTR point to the same buffer; for short packets KSGEN is triggered no later than RADIO START (for example from READY through PPI) with the ENDKSGEN-to-CRYPT shortcut on. When receiving, CCM INPTR equals RADIO PACKETPTR, KSGEN is triggered no later than START, and CRYPT no earlier than the RADIO ADDRESS event; triggered exactly then, decryption is finished by the RADIO END event. Extended-length packets need the keystream started earlier, for example at TXEN or RXEN. Bus collisions between the CPU and EasyDMA masters on one RAM block can upset on-the-fly operation and raise ERROR.

COMP compares VIN+ from one of AIN0 to AIN7 (chosen in PSEL) with VIN-, over an input range of 0 V to VDD. In differential mode VIN- is another AIN pin (EXTREFSEL), with optional hysteresis VDIFFHYST (HYST register). In single-ended mode VIN- comes from a 64-level reference ladder fed by VREF, which is VDD, an AIN pin (AREF via EXTREFSEL) or an internal 1.2 V, 1.8 V or 2.4 V reference (REFSEL); thresholds VUP and VDOWN set in TH give the hysteresis, VIN- switching to VDOWN once the output is ABOVE and back to VUP once BELOW, and HYST is ignored. Low-power, normal and high-speed modes trade current for response time. After ENABLE, START starts it and READY follows after tINT_REF,START with an internal reference or tCOMP,START otherwise; STOP stops it. Events: UP, DOWN, CROSS (either direction) and READY; SAMPLE copies the output to RESULT. The required registers are set before ENABLE, and COMP must be stopped before it is disabled. COMP and SAADC can run together but not on the same pin, and COMP shares ID 26 with LPCOMP.

An optional current source (ISOURCE) on the selected VIN+ pin sinks current while the output is high and sources it while low, turning the comparator into a relaxation oscillator for single-pin capacitive sensing with the sensor from the pin to ground; it works in any mode. With 10 µA, VUP - VDOWN of 1 V and about 10 pF, it oscillates near 500 kHz.

Arm TrustZone CryptoCell 312, in the application core, provides root of trust and cryptographic services: a TRNG (NIST 800-90B, AIS-31, FIPS 140-2), an AES-based PRNG (NIST 800-90A), RSA up to 3072-bit keys (PKCS#1 v2.1/v1.5, optional CRT), ECC on NIST P-192 to P-521, SEC 2 secp160r1 to secp521r1, Koblitz secp160k1 to secp256k1, Ed25519 and Curve25519 with ECDH/ECDSA, SRP up to 3072 bits, SHA-1, SHA-2 up to 256 bits and HMAC, AES with 128- and 256-bit keys (modes: GCM, CTR, CBC, ECB, CCM/CCM*, CMAC/CBC-MAC), and ChaCha20/Poly1305 AEAD with 128- and 256-bit keys. It takes keys over a dedicated bus from the KMU. Its ENABLE register switches it on, and its functions are used through the SDK library. While enabled the device cannot reach the System ON all-idle state. Its DMA works on memory-mapped regions without the CPU, transfers up to 2^16-1 bytes, sets the security attribute of its bus transactions, and needs data it cannot reach copied first to memory it can.

DCNF gives each core its CPU ID (CPUID reads 0x00000000 in the application core and 0x00000001 in the network core) and, in the application core, protects its AHB multilayer interconnect: EXTPERI[0].PROTECT, EXTRAM[0].PROTECT (one bit per RAM slave, eight in all) and EXTCODE[0].PROTECT block paths from masters in the other core to local peripherals, RAM and code. A blocked access raises a BusFault or HardFault, according to BUSFAULTENA in the Cortex-M33 SHCSR. The network core DCNF has no PROTECT registers.

DPPI lets peripherals trigger each other's tasks from events with no CPU involvement and with precise timing. Every peripheral has one SUBSCRIBE register per task and one PUBLISH register per event, each holding a channel index and an enable bit; an index naming a channel that does not exist gives unpredictable results. A channel can link a single event to a single task, fan one event out to several tasks, gather several events into one task, or mix both; events published on one channel at the same instant merge into one. The DPPI controller (DPPIC) enables channels globally, one by one through CHEN, CHENSET and CHENCLR, or by group through the CHG[n].EN and CHG[n].DIS tasks, which can themselves subscribe to channels; enable wins over disable when both hit a channel together. CHG[x] can be written only while both its subscribe registers are disabled. Each core's DPPIC has 32 channels and 6 channel groups.

The application core DPPIC has split security, with each channel made secure or non-secure in SPU.DPPI.PERM. A non-secure peripheral can only publish or subscribe on non-secure channels; a secure one can use all of them. A group is secure if any of its channels is. Non-secure accesses to bits or groups covering secure channels are ignored on write and read as zero, with no exception raised. A non-secure group ignores events from a secure channel; a secure group can subscribe to either kind.

ECB, in the network core, performs AES-128 block encryption (no decryption) for jobs such as hashes, signatures and keystreams. ECBDATAPTR points at a Data RAM structure holding the key, the cleartext and room for the ciphertext; STARTECB loads key and data by EasyDMA, and ENDECB follows once the ciphertext is written back. STOPECB aborts. It shares the AES core with CCM and AAR at the lowest priority: if the core is busy, or a conflict arises, the operation is aborted with ERRORECB. Its DMA reaches only RAM.

An EGU lets firmware or DPPI raise interrupts and events for signalling between priority levels, for example to run part of a high-priority handler at a lower priority. Each instance has its own interrupt vector and 16 TRIGGER tasks, each setting its matching TRIGGERED event, so one interrupt can carry up to 16 flags. The application core has EGU0 to EGU5, the network core EGU0.

The application core Cortex-M33 FPU exception signals appear as events in the FPU peripheral: FPUIOC as INVALIDOPERATION, FPUIDC as DENORMALINPUT, FPUOFC as OVERFLOW, FPUUFC as UNDERFLOW, FPUDZC as DIVIDEBYZERO and FPUIXC as INEXACT, each able to raise an interrupt. The exception source is cleared by writing 0 to the FPSCR.

General purpose pins are grouped in ports of up to 32 pins; how many ports and pins exist depends on the package. Each pin has its own output drive setting, pull-up and pull-down, high- or low-level wakeup sense, and can raise interrupts on change, be driven through DPPI and GPIOTE channels, and be routed to any peripheral's signals. A LATCH register records SENSE hits. Pins can be shared among the cores and are given secure or non-secure attributes together with the SPU.

Each pin belongs to the application core, the network core, a peripheral with dedicated pins, or the trace and debug subsystem, chosen by the MCUSEL field of the application core's PIN_CNF[n] (writable from secure code only). All pins start on the application core. Only the owning core can drive, read or set a pin as analog: reads from another core return zero and its writes are ignored. A pin given to a subsystem that cannot reach it stays with the application core's GPIO. Every core's GPIO has its own independent register set. MCUSEL should be changed only while the pin is disabled, to avoid glitches. While a pin is not on the application core, that core's LATCH bit, MCUSEL and SENSE for the pin ignore writes and read 0.

Each of PIN0 to PIN31 is set up in its PIN_CNF[n] register: direction, drive strength, pull-up or pull-down, sense, input buffer connect, and analog input on the pins that have one. All writable GPIO registers are retained. The input buffer can be disconnected to save power when a pin is not an input; it must be connected for IN to read the pin and for sensing to work. Other peripherals can take over a pin's output and configuration or read its digital or analog level. Not every pin supports every drive setting. A pad's level reaches IN after 2 CPU clock cycles, and after DETECT has gone high the pad must return to its inactive level for 3 CPU clock cycles before a new DETECT can arise. A digital input held between VIL and VIH for long periods should be avoided.

Each pin can be set to sense a high or a low level, and raises its own DETECT when that level is present. By default (DETECTMODE) the DETECT of every pin in the port is ORed into one port DETECT signal, used by other peripherals; this works in System ON and System OFF. DETECT rises at once if a pin already meets its SENSE condition when sensing is enabled, which gives a PORT event if DETECT was low, so the pin should sit at a non-triggering level first. DETECT also wakes the device from System OFF and gives the GPIOTE PORT event (GPIOTE_SEC for secure pins). DETECTMODE governs non-secure pins and DETECTMODE_SEC secure pins.

When a pin's DETECT goes high the matching LATCH bit is set (PIN0 sets bit 0). A LATCH bit clears only when the CPU writes 1 to it, and not while that pin's DETECT is still high; DETECT falling does not clear it. LDETECT is high while any LATCH bit is 1 and low once all are cleared; if bits remain set after a clear, LDETECT gives a new rising edge. The CPU can read LATCH at any time to see which pins met their SENSE condition, even after the condition has gone and whether or not LDETECT is in use. DETECTMODE can make the port DETECT follow LDETECT instead of the ORed pin signals.

GPIO is a split-security peripheral. A non-secure access can configure and drive only pins marked non-secure in SPU GPIOPORT.PERM; for a secure pin, non-secure writes to OUT, OUTSET, OUTCLR, DIR, DIRSET, DIRCLR, LATCH, PIN[i].OUT and PIN_CNF[i] have no effect on that pin's bit, and non-secure reads of those registers and IN return 0 for it, with no exception raised. DETECTMODE_SEC selects the source of DETECT_SEC for secure pins and reads 0 and ignores writes from non-secure code; DETECTMODE selects the source of DETECT_NSEC for non-secure pins. DETECT_NSEC goes to GPIOTE and DETECT_SEC to GPIOTESEC, so each raises events and interrupts for its own pins.

GPIOTE gives pins tasks and events. Each channel is tied to one pin: a pin change can raise an event that drives tasks over DPPI, and DPPI events can drive the pin. Each channel has up to three output tasks, SET and CLR fixed and OUT set by CONFIG[n].POLARITY to set, clear or toggle, and one IN event on a rising edge, falling edge or any change. Pin changes can be detected at low power in System ON and System OFF.

The secure GPIOTE instance can act on any pin chosen in CONFIG[n].PSEL; the non-secure instance can choose only non-secure pins. While a channel's task or event controls a pin, only GPIOTE sets its output and writes through GPIO have no effect; when released, the pin takes its GPIO settings again. Event mode makes the pin an input and Task mode an output, both overriding GPIO DIR (and OUT for Task mode); Disabled leaves the pin to its PIN_CNF. OUTINIT gives the pin's starting level in Task mode. MODE=Disabled differs from MODE=Task with POLARITY=None: in the latter, a SET or CLR in the same cycle as OUT leaves the pin unchanged. A pin may be given to only one channel at a time.

PORT is raised on the rising edge of the GPIO DETECT signal and so can come from many pins. DETECT_SEC serves the secure GPIOTE instance and DETECT_NONSEC the non-secure one. DETECT that is already high when the system enters System ON IDLE will not wake it, so all DETECT sources should be cleared before sleep; with LATCH as the source, bits still set after a clear give a new rising edge. Entering System OFF with DETECT high wakes the device at once through a System OFF reset. PORT can wake the CPU from WFI or WFE with everything else idle, the lowest System ON current. To configure sources without a spurious interrupt: disable the PORT interrupt (INTENCLR.PORT), set PIN_CNF[n].SENSE, write 0 to EVENTS_PORT, then enable the interrupt (INTENSET.PORT).

In Event mode, setting LATENCY to LowPower cuts current for both the PORT and IN events; the pins must have PIN_CNF[n].SENSE set. For IN, SENSE must match the polarity: High for LoToHi, Low for HiToLo. For PORT, SENSE may have any value. POLARITY=Toggle needs LATENCY=LowLatency.

The I2S interface streams audio in master or slave mode, transmitting and receiving at once, in the original two-channel I2S format or left- or right-aligned, with 32, 24, 16 or 8-bit samples, sample width separate from word width, and a low-jitter master clock generator for a range of sample rates. EasyDMA moves samples to and from RAM. Its signals are MCK, LRCK, SCK, SDIN and SDOUT.

The master supplies LRCK and SCK to the slave. Data shifts with SCK and LRCK: SDOUT changes on the falling SCK edge and SDIN is sampled on the rising edge, MSB first. In master mode the first frame sent after start is zeros. TX and RX are enabled separately (CONFIG.TXEN, CONFIG.RXEN) and run in either mode. START begins streaming; with TX on, TXPTRUPD comes just before each RXTXD.MAXCNT words have gone out, and with RX on, RXPTRUPD comes just after each RXTXD.MAXCNT words have come in. FRAMESTART marks the active LRCK edge at the start of a frame after MAXCNT words, the first at the first active LRCK edge after START; it is only given for whole left-right pairs.

LRCK (word clock) frames the data and its frequency equals the sample rate. In I2S format the left sample goes in the low half of LRCK and the right in the high half; in Aligned format the left sample is in the high half. In mono the unused half carries zeros. LRCK toggles around the falling edge of SCK. SCK pulses once per data bit. In master mode both are derived from MCK; in slave mode SCK comes from the external master. MCK comes from the source set in CONFIG.CLKCONFIG and CONFIG.MCKFREQ; the generator adds no jitter, is enabled by CONFIG.MCKEN and runs between the START and STOP tasks. It must be on in master mode and may be on in slave mode to supply an external master. MCK can be retuned while running: with PCLK32M through MCKFREQ, with ACLK by adjusting the audio clock. SCK may never exceed MCK, and the MCK/LRCK ratio must be a multiple of 2 × CONFIG.SWIDTH. MCK can be put on a pin (PSEL.MCK) for devices that need it; in slave mode the I2S does not use MCK.

The master clock generator runs from the 32 MHz peripheral clock PCLK32M (synchronous to HFCLK) or from the audio PLL clock ACLK with configurable frequency, chosen in CONFIG.CLKCONFIG. Running PCLK32M from HFXO rather than HFINT is recommended for MCK accuracy and jitter; ACLK requires HFXO. The BYPASS field of CONFIG.CLKCONFIG takes MCK straight from the source.

CONFIG.SWIDTH sets both the sample width in memory and the SCK cycles per half-frame; a half-frame can be wider than the sample, with more SCK pulses than sample bits. CONFIG.FORMAT picks Aligned, where the first bit of a half-frame is sampled on the first rising SCK after the LRCK edge, or I2S, where it is the second rising edge (one bit of delay). Where half-frame and sample widths differ, CONFIG.ALIGN places the sample left (half-frame starts with the MSB) or right (half-frame ends with the LSB).

In slave mode the half-frame need not match the sample width. Left-aligned with extra SCK pulses: received bits after the LSB are dropped and transmitted bits after the LSB are 0. Left-aligned with too few pulses: data is truncated, LSBs first. Right-aligned with extra pulses: received bits before the MSB are dropped and transmitted bits after the LSB are 0. Right-aligned with too few pulses: received data is sign-extended to the sample width and transmitted data is truncated, LSBs first.

TXD.PTR and RXD.PTR give the TX source and RX destination in Data RAM; memory is touched only for the direction enabled. Both pointers are double-buffered and taken over every RXTXD.MAXCNT words, raising TXPTRUPD and RXPTRUPD. A pointer outside Data RAM can cause a HardFault or memory corruption. One RXTXD.MAXCNT, counted in 32-bit words, sizes both buffers, since TX and RX move the same number of samples. Each 32-bit word carries a single 32-bit sample, a single 24-bit sample (right-aligned, sign-extended), a pair of 16-bit samples or four 8-bit ones. For stereo, samples sit in memory as left-right pairs, left in the lower part; in mono (CONFIG.CHANNELS Left or Right) only the chosen channel's RX samples are stored, and each TX sample is sent on both left and right.

A typical start: set the CONFIG registers (RXEN, TXEN, MCKEN, MCKFREQ, RATIO, SWIDTH, ALIGN, FORMAT, CHANNELS), map the pins in the PSEL registers, set TXD.PTR, RXD.PTR and the buffer size, write ENABLE = 1, trigger START, then on each TXPTRUPD and RXPTRUPD write the next buffer pointer and clear the event. MCKFREQ set to 32 MHz/8 (4 MHz) with RATIO 256 gives 15.625 ks/s.

MCK, SCK, LRCK, SDIN and SDOUT go to the pins in the PSEL registers and are taken when ENABLE is set; the I2S then sets each pin's direction, overriding GPIO. In System OFF and while the I2S is disabled the pins take their GPIO settings, so the levels wanted there must be set in GPIO.

Each MCU has its own IPC peripheral to send events to and receive events from the others. An instance has several SEND tasks and RECEIVE events: SEND_CNF[n] picks which IPC channels SEND[n] signals, and RECEIVE_CNF[n] which channels raise RECEIVE[n]; either can reach every channel. Events on one channel less than tIPC apart may merge into one, so one can be lost; using a separate channel for acknowledgements avoids this. An IPC event carries no data; data is passed in shared memory, for example as a mailbox or command queue, and software gives each channel its meaning. SEND and RECEIVE can be wired through DPPI, so a peripheral event in one MCU (a TIMER COMPARE, say) can trigger a task in another (a TIMER CAPTURE) with no CPU. The GPMEM registers are free storage, private to each instance and retained only in System ON. There are 16 SEND tasks, 16 RECEIVE events and 16 channels per instance.

The key management unit enforces access rules on a region of UICR that holds key slots the CPU cannot read unless allowed. There are 128 slots, each holding one 128-bit key value together with the rules for its use and the address it is sent to; longer keys span several slots. A slot can push its key over a dedicated secure APB straight into a write-only key register of an accelerator such as CryptoCell, so the CPU uses the key without seeing it. The KMU and the key slots are reachable from secure mode only; even when the KMU is set non-secure, every non-secure transaction is blocked.

UICR is split into a one-time-programmable (OTP) region and a key storage region. OTP is emulated by allowing each halfword to be written once. Key storage holds the slots, each a key header and a key value; key headers take 0x400 of address space, room for 128 slots. The region is meant for keys with a lifetime, not per-session keys negotiated with CPU involvement. A hardware state machine admits or blocks each transaction by its security and the register type: key headers can always be read, while writes, and reads of key values, need a slot selected through the KMU; a blocked access returns 0xDEADDEAD on the AHB. The state machine works on one slot at a time.

Writing an implementation-defined 32-bit word into the UICR ERASEPROTECT register permanently disables erase of UICR, by internal NVMC.ERASEALL and by ERASEALL through CTRL-AP. For field returns, secure boot code can run an authenticated channel over the CTRL-AP mailbox and then re-enable CTRL-AP ERASEALL for a while.

Only a halfword still reading 0xFFFF can be written, and only by a secure AHB write of a full 32-bit word; halfwords can be written together or one at a time, with the other halfword masked as 0xFFFF. For example, writing 0x1234FFFF to a location holding 0xFFFFAABB leaves 0x1234AABB. A write breaking these rules is ignored and sets STATUS.BLOCKED.

Key storage can hold symmetric keys, hashes, key pairs and other device secrets, usable in cryptography without being revealed. A slot's header carries its permissions and, if wanted, a secure address to push the key to. By default every slot holds a 128-bit value of all 1s, with no destination and no restrictions.

A slot is used only after its ID is written to SELECTKEYSLOT; IDs run from 1 to 128, and 0 (the reset value) selects none. UICR KEYSLOT.KEY[N] and KEYSLOT.CONFIG[N] belong to slot ID N+1. SELECTKEYSLOT should go back to 0 when a slot is finished with. STATUS.SELECTED is set when the selected slot is read or written successfully; STATUS.BLOCKED is set by any access to another slot, a failed selection or any access violation, which normal use never causes. STATUS resets on every write to SELECTKEYSLOT.

Select an empty slot; if it is to be pushed, write the recipient's address to KEYSLOT.CONFIG[ID-1].DEST; write the 128-bit value to KEYSLOT.KEY[ID-1].VALUE[0-3]; write the permissions to KEYSLOT.CONFIG[ID-1].PERM; select slot 0. Longer keys repeat this per 128-bit segment, with the same header settings and each destination address 4 words (128 bits) above the last. A readable slot that will not use DEST should have push disabled. Flash writes must be enabled in NVMC CONFIG for the duration. The steps are blocked with no slot selected, a non-empty slot, a non-empty NVM destination, or a write to another slot's VALUE registers.

A slot set readable can be read directly from the UICR map: select it, read KEYSLOT.KEY[ID-1].VALUE[0-3] if its STATE and READ permissions allow, then select slot 0. Readable keys suit secure boot, where the CPU checks integrity anyway, and key types with no hardware peripheral to receive them. The read returns 0xDEADDEAD with no slot selected, a slot not readable, a revoked slot, or a read of another slot's VALUE registers.

A non-readable slot is used by pushing it over the secure APB to the address in its DEST register, typically a write-only key register of an accelerator: select the slot, trigger TASKS_PUSH_KEYSLOT, wait for EVENTS_KEYSLOT_PUSHED once the 128-bit value is delivered, then select slot 0. Each slot of a multi-slot key is pushed on its own. EVENTS_KEYSLOT_ERROR follows instead with no slot selected, no destination set, an error from flash or the peripheral, push disabled, or default permissions; EVENTS_KEYSLOT_REVOKED follows for a revoked slot.

Writing the STATE field of KEYSLOT.CONFIG[ID-1].PERM revokes a slot: the KMU zeroes its VALUE registers, a push gives EVENTS_KEYSLOT_REVOKED, and a read returns the fixed value 3735936685. Keys already pushed into a peripheral's key register stay usable there until secure code disables or resets that peripheral.

The low-power comparator compares one of the analog inputs AIN0 to AIN7 (VIN+, chosen by PSEL) against a reference (VIN-): one of two external reference pins, AIN0 or AIN1 (EXTREFSEL), or a 15-step internal ladder in sixteenths of VDD (REFSEL). Inputs span 0 to VDD and hysteresis is optional. It works in System ON and System OFF and can wake the device from either. LPCOMP and COMP cannot be started at the same time.

PSEL, REFSEL, EXTREFSEL and HYST must be set before ENABLE. START begins a comparison and READY follows after tSTARTUP, when the output is valid. Each rise of VIN+ above VIN- gives UP and CROSS; each fall gives DOWN and CROSS. With hysteresis on, the up threshold is VIN- + VHYST/2 and the down threshold VIN- - VHYST/2. STOP ends it, and it must be stopped before ENABLE is cleared. SAMPLE copies the present output to RESULT. System OFF may not be entered while a READY event is still due. While enabled, all its registers are retained, but they reset on wakeup from System OFF. The ANADETECT signal, derived from the UP, DOWN or CROSS condition as set in the ANADETECT register, wakes the device from System OFF; that wakeup gives no events. LPCOMP shares analog resources with the SAADC and the two can run together, but not on the same input pin. It also shares registers with peripherals of the same ID. The selected analog pins are taken when it is enabled.

MUTEX holds 16 one-bit locks for resources shared between the CPUs. Reading an unlocked MUTEX[i] locks it and returns 0; reading a locked one returns 1 and leaves it locked. Writing 0 to a locked mutex unlocks it; writing 0 to an unlocked one does nothing. A CPU takes a lock by reading until it gets 0 and frees it by writing 0; if two loads coincide, bus arbitration gives the lock to one. The peripheral does not handle faults: a mutex held when a fault occurs stays locked unless the fault handler frees it.

NFCT is an NFC-A listening device (tag) to the NFC Forum definition: a 13.56 MHz AM receiver and load modulator at 106 kbps, with low-power wake-on-field detection (SENSE), hardware framing and deframing of NFC-A frames, a programmable frame timing controller, and automatic collision resolution, CRC and parity. Frame data moves by EasyDMA; an event marks each frame sent or received, and received frames are deframed with their data part written to RAM.

In SENSE mode, in System ON or System OFF, the field detector watches for a reader. In System ON, FIELDDETECTED is raised when the antenna energy passes a threshold, and FIELDLOST when the field becomes too weak to communicate. In System OFF the field detector wakes the device through a reset (seen in RESETREAS); entering System OFF with a field already present wakes it at once. The reset disables NFCT, so the reset handler must activate and configure it again. HFXO must run before NFCT enters the ACTIVATED state; calibration happens on the ACTIVATE task, and HFXO may be stopped in SENSE mode. The FIELDDETECTED_ACTIVATE shortcut can be used if HFXO is already running in SENSE mode. FIELDLOST is not raised in SENSE mode; a SENSE task while a field is present gives no FIELDDETECTED; and a FIELDDETECTED cleared before ACTIVATE appears again after it, which the FIELDDETECTED_ACTIVATE shortcut avoids.

Tasks and finished operations move NFCT between states, and events report them. From DISABLE, SENSE leads to SENSE_FIELD and ACTIVATE to IDLERU, which gives READY on reaching IDLE (with automatic collision resolution) or ACTIVE_A (without it). With collision resolution on, an ALL_REQ or SENS_REQ from IDLE or SLEEP_A starts it (AUTOCOLRESSTARTED) and passes through READY_A or READY_A* to ACTIVE_A (SELECTED); another command gives COLLISION and a return; SLP_REQ from ACTIVE_A leads to SLEEP_A. GOIDLE and GOSLEEP force IDLE and SLEEP_A. In ACTIVE_A, ENABLERXDATA leads to RECEIVE, ending with RXFRAMEEND or RXERROR, and STARTTX to TRANSMIT, ending with TXFRAMEEND. DISABLE returns to DISABLE from any state.

The antenna connects to two pins shared with GPIO. The PROTECT field of UICR NFCPINS, reloaded at every reset, sets their use. With PROTECT=NFC a protection circuit shorts the two pins together when their difference exceeds about 2 V, guarding against strong fields, and the GPIO function is off. With PROTECT=Disabled there is no such protection and NFCT never leaves the DISABLE state. Used as GPIO, these pins have higher capacitance (CPAD_NFC) and leak between each other (INFC_LEAK) when driven to different levels, so both should be set to the same level before entering a power-saving mode.

NFCT reads or writes Data RAM through one pointer, PACKETPTR, but not both at once. RXFRAMESTART and RXFRAMEEND bracket the RAM writes of a received frame, TXFRAMESTART and TXFRAMEEND the reads of a transmitted one. If a transmit and a receive are requested together the transmit wins; starting a transfer while another is running is unpredictable, so the end event of the one in progress should be awaited. MAXLEN caps the bytes moved; a frame longer than MAXLEN is cut short, and in RX that sets FRAMESTATUS.RX OVERRUN and raises RXERROR. RXD.AMOUNT and TXD.AMOUNT count data bytes and bits without SoF, EoF and parity, but RXD.AMOUNT includes the CRC. A new PACKETPTR for RX takes effect only with ENABLERXDATA. A PACKETPTR outside Data RAM can cause a hard fault or RAM corruption. Receive and transmit frames usually alternate, so the next transmit's pointer, size, TXD.FRAMECONFIG and TXD.AMOUNT may be written while a receive runs, and the next receive's pointer, size and RXD.FRAMECONFIG while a transmit runs, as soon as the frame's STARTED event has come; changing the frame configuration of the frame in progress is unpredictable. The least significant bit of the least significant byte goes on air first, and bytes sit in RAM in rising address order.

In ACTIVE_A, to transmit, software sets PACKETPTR and MAXLEN (matching the frame size) and triggers STARTTX; STARTED shows both registers have been taken. The assembler reads TXD.AMOUNT.TXDATABYTES bytes, plus one more if TXDATABITS is above 0, and builds a frame of (8 × TXDATABYTES + TXDATABITS) bits as TXD.FRAMECONFIG directs, adding SoF, parity and an on-the-fly CRC when set, so the frame on air is longer than TXD.AMOUNT. It can build short, standard and bit-oriented SDD frames. Bytes go out in RAM order, each LSB (b0) first. DISCARDMODE chooses whether the first bits of the first byte or the last bits of the last byte are dropped when TXDATABITS is not zero; with PARITY = Parity and DiscardStart a parity bit follows the incomplete first byte, but none follows an incomplete last byte. Bits are numbered b0 to b7. The frame timing controller sets exactly when the frame goes out.

To receive in ACTIVE_A, software sets PACKETPTR and MAXLEN, then triggers ENABLERXDATA; STARTED shows they have been taken. RXFRAMESTART marks an incoming frame, whose data is written to RAM with parity, SoF and EoF checked and stripped as RXD.FRAMECONFIG sets; the CRC, when enabled, is checked and also written to RAM. At EoF, RXFRAMEEND is raised and RXD.AMOUNT gives the bytes and bits received. The content is not interpreted beyond SoF, EoF, parity and CRC. The gap from one frame's end to the next one's start may be only 86 µs, so PACKETPTR, MAXLEN and ENABLERXDATA must be ready promptly after the previous frame; a shortcut from TXFRAMEEND to ENABLERXDATA is recommended.

A counter tracks 13.56 MHz carrier periods since the end of the last received frame's EoF, corrected by the last received data bit as NFC-A defines. With FRAMEDELAYMODE = Window, a STARTTX before the count reaches FRAMEDELAYMIN is held until it does, and one between FRAMEDELAYMIN and FRAMEDELAYMAX goes at once. With ExactVal, transmission is held until the count equals FRAMEDELAYMAX. WindowGrid is like Window but starts on the NFC-A listen bit grid (slots of 128 carrier periods). Reaching FRAMEDELAYMAX with no STARTTX raises ERROR with FRAMEDELAYTIMEOUT in ERRORSTATUS, even where no response was due, including commands handled by collision resolution that need no reply. FRAMEDELAYMIN and FRAMEDELAYMAX may only be changed before STARTTX.

Automatic collision resolution is on by default and recommended (less power and simpler software); the MODE field of AUTOCOLRESCONFIG turns it off, after which every command arrives through EasyDMA. SENSRES and SELRES must be set beforehand, together with NFCID1_LAST for a 4-byte ID, NFCID1_2ND_LAST as well for 7 bytes, and NFCID1_3RD_LAST as well for 10 bytes. FICR NFC.TAGHEADER0..3 hold a valid NFCID1 that software can copy in. Hardware handles the states from IDLE to ACTIVE_A: AUTOCOLRESSTARTED when it begins, SELECTED on reaching ACTIVE_A, COLLISION if it fails. Other events (ERROR, RXERROR and more) may appear meanwhile and should be ignored except COLLISION, SELECTED and FIELDLOST; unwanted shortcuts should be disabled during it. Frames with CRC or parity errors in ACTIVE_A restart it unless it is turned off there. SLP_REQ is handled automatically but, having no response, gives an ERROR with FRAMEDELAYTIMEOUT, to be ignored until SELECTED and then cleared.

In the ACTIVATED state an amplitude regulator holds the antenna swing within the Vswing limit. The antenna coil connects differentially between NFC1 and NFC2, with two external capacitors tuning the circuit to 13.56 MHz. A 2 µH antenna gives tuning capacitors of about 130 pF on each pin, and the total capacitance on NFC1 and NFC2 must match.

In a strong NFC field, current can flow backwards into the supply through parasitic diodes and ESD structures. A battery that cannot accept reverse current needs a series diode between it and the device.

NFCT drives a loop antenna directly, receiving through its internal front end and answering by changing its input resistance, which the reader sees as load modulation. It can also put the digital modulation signal on a GPIO for an external front end or antenna; reception still uses the internal front end, and transmission can use the internal front end (default), the external one, or both. MODULATIONCTRL and MODULATIONPSEL set this and must be written before NFCT answers a reader, ideally at start-up and each time NFCT powers up. The pin must be a GPIO output, and its GPIO.OUT level is driven while NFCT is disabled. While idle the pin is low; while answering, NFCT switches an 847 kHz subcarrier, divided down from the carrier, on and off on it (OOK).

The NVMC writes and erases the internal flash and UICR. It is split-security: configured non-secure, non-secure code reaches only some registers; configured secure, only secure code reaches it. Writing needs CONFIG.WEN and erasing CONFIG.EEN, never both at once. Secure code uses CONFIG for secure regions and CONFIGNS for non-secure ones; non-secure code uses CONFIGNS and reaches non-secure regions only.

Flash is written one full 32-bit word at a time to a word-aligned address; byte or halfword writes give a bus fault. A write can only turn 1s into 0s. One address can be written nWRITE times before its page must be erased; to write fewer than 32 bits, the bits to keep are written as 1. A word takes tWRITE, and a CPU fetching code from flash meanwhile is stalled.

With erase enabled (CONFIG for secure pages, CONFIGNS for non-secure ones), writing 0xFFFFFFFF to the first word of a code-area page erases it to all 1s in tERASEPAGE; this does not work on UICR. The CPU stalls if it runs from flash meanwhile. A page erase can also be split into shorter partial erases.

operation.topic: NVMC UICR writes and erase all
operation.text: UICR is written like flash, takes effect only after a reset, and is reachable from secure code only (non-secure writes fault). It can be written nWRITE times before an ERASEALL. To lock the chip after loading non-secure code, set UICR to protect secure code, then through the non-secure debugger use WRITEUICRNS to set APPROTECT, which the NVMC writes as 0x00000000. With erase enabled, ERASEALL clears all flash and UICR, but not FICR, in tERASEALL; the UICR protection bits can block it.

operation.topic: NVMC non-secure programming and power-fail protection
operation.text: Non-secure code programs non-secure flash through CONFIGNS (CONFIG for non-secure transactions), READY and READYNEXT. Erase and write are both write transactions, so the SPU keeps non-secure code from writing a secure page. With the power-fail comparator on and the supply below VPOF, writes and erases are prevented: a warning at the start of an operation blocks it with a bus error; a warning during a write lets that write finish, and later writes are blocked with a bus error while it lasts.

An instruction cache can be enabled on the ICODE bus. A hit costs 0 wait states; a miss costs a number that depends on CPU frequency (W_FLASHCACHE). The cache can raise performance and, when the saving in flash accesses outweighs its own current, lower average current. Disabled, it draws no current and keeps no contents. ICACHECNF can enable profiling, counting hits in IHIT and misses in IMISS. The application core NVMC lacks this cache (ICACHECNF, IHIT and IMISS), and the network core NVMC lacks the TrustZone registers WRITEUICRNS and CONFIGNS.

The PDM interface takes pulse-density-modulated audio from external front ends such as digital microphones: up to two microphones as a left-right pair on one data line. It generates the PDM clock, decimates in hardware to 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz, with a PDM_CLK to sample-rate ratio of 64 or 80, and streams continuously to RAM through EasyDMA. Its signals are CLK and DIN.

MCLKCONFIG picks the master clock source, the 32 MHz peripheral clock PCLK32M (synchronous to HFCLK) or the audio PLL clock ACLK, and may only be changed while PDM is stopped. Running PCLK32M from HFXO rather than HFINT is recommended for accuracy and jitter; ACLK requires HFXO. The generator adds no jitter and PDMCLKCTRL sets the PDM clock frequency. The frequency can be changed while running: with PCLK32M through PDMCLKCTRL, with ACLK by adjusting the audio clock.

By default the left microphone's bits are sampled on the falling edge of PDM_CLK and the right's on the rising edge; the EDGE field of MODE swaps them. Each bitstream goes through its own filter that converts it to 16-bit PCM and decimates it by the RATIO (64 or 80), giving two 16-bit samples per output period. Each channel then has a volume control spanning -20 dB to +20 dB about the reset gain GPDM,default, set by GAINL and GAINR in 0.5 dB steps within MinGain and MaxGain. START and STOP run and end the stream; STOP takes effect after the current frame, and STOPPED then shows all activity, DMA included, is done. Restarting before STOPPED is unpredictable.

To get 2500 RMS output counts from a 1 kHz, 90 dBA tone into a microphone of -26 dBFS sensitivity, add the module's default gain to the gain of the microphone and acoustic path and shift GAINL and GAINR by that sum. If only the module's gain matters, GAINL and GAINR are set to -GPDM,default; with GPDM,default = 3.2 dB the nearest 0.5 dB step is 3.0 dB, so GAINL = GAINR = DefaultGain - (2 × 3).

Samples go straight to RAM at SAMPLE.PTR, little-endian; a pointer outside Data RAM can cause a HardFault or RAM corruption. The buffer is one block of SAMPLE.MAXCNT 16-bit samples, so it takes SAMPLE.MAXCNT × 2 bytes; in stereo it holds alternating left and right samples (half the time span of mono), in mono only left samples. Start with START after SAMPLE.PTR and SAMPLE.MAXCNT are written. The filters take time to settle and the microphone may produce transients, so the first samples (typically about 50) may be invalid and are best discarded. SAMPLE.PTR is double-buffered: after STARTED the next pointer can be written; END marks a full buffer, after which capture continues into the new one with another STARTED.

One microphone (mono) connects its clock to CLK and its data to DIN; depending on the microphone, either the left channel (sampled on the falling CLK edge) or the right (rising edge) carries valid data. With two microphones, one is set left and the other right by tying its L/R pin high or to ground, and microphones of exactly the same make and type are strongly recommended so their left and right timing match.

CLK and DIN go to the pins in PSEL.CLK and PSEL.DIN; with CONNECT set to Disconnected the signal reaches no pin and PDM does not work. These settings apply only while PDM is enabled and are kept only in System ON; when PDM is disabled the pins act as plain GPIO with their OUT and PIN_CNF settings. The pins should be set up in GPIO before PDM is enabled, and kept so for as long as the external circuit is attached, so they stay driven correctly while PDM is disabled or the device is in System OFF. Only one peripheral may drive a given pin.

Each PWM module counts with one 15-bit counter, upward or upward then downward, and drives four pin channels that share one period but each with its own duty cycle and polarity, edge- or centre-aligned. Duty-cycle sequences in RAM are fetched by EasyDMA without the CPU and without glitches; polarity, duty cycle and base frequency can change every period, and sequences can repeat or be chained into loops. The application core has PWM0 to PWM3.

COUNTERTOP with the PWM_CLK PRESCALER sets the period; MODE picks up or up-and-down counting. A COUNTERTOP below a compare value gives no edges, with OUT[n] held high for FallingEdge polarity. The compare registers are internal and are loaded only through the decoder. COUNTERTOP may be written at any time; it is ignored when DECODER.LOAD = WaveForm (taken from RAM instead), and otherwise is sampled on SEQSTART[n] and whenever a new RAM value loads. In up mode the counter resets to zero at COUNTERTOP and OUT[n] inverts, giving edge-aligned pulses; a compare of 0 holds OUT[n] low and one of COUNTERTOP holds it high (FallingEdge). In up-and-down mode the counter turns at COUNTERTOP and counts down, and OUT[n] inverts at the second compare match, giving centre-aligned pulses. A PRESCALER of DIV_1 with COUNTERTOP = 16000 gives a 1 ms period.

The decoder reads sequences of 16-bit halfwords from RAM by EasyDMA into the compare registers. In each halfword, bit 15 sets polarity (0 RisingEdge: the first edge of the period rises; 1 FallingEdge) and bits 14:0 are the compare value. DECODER.LOAD sets the layout: Common (one value for all four channels), Grouped (one value for COMP0 and COMP1, the next for COMP2 and COMP3), Single (one value per channel), or WaveForm (values for OUT[0] to OUT[2] and a fourth halfword loaded into COUNTERTOP, so up to three channels with a period that changes every cycle, for arbitrary waveforms such as LED lighting). SEQ[n].PTR points at the sequence in RAM (outside RAM risks a HardFault or RAM corruption) and SEQ[n].CNT gives its length in halfwords; Grouped needs one halfword per group and Single one per channel. A sequence in use must have CNT > 0.

SEQ[n].REFRESH = N loads a new value every N+1 periods (0 means every period, within the minimum period). With DECODER.MODE = NextStep, REFRESH and ENDDELAY are ignored and each NEXTSTEP task loads the next value at the next period. If PWM is idle, SEQSTART[n] loads the first value and starts generation; SEQSTARTED[n] follows once the first value is read and running. With LOOP.CNT = 0 a sequence plays once, SEQEND[n] comes when its last value starts, and the output then holds the last value. STOP ends generation at the end of the running period, raises STOPPED and leaves the pins at their GPIO OUT idle level; only SEQSTART[n] restarts it, from the first value. With LOOP.CNT > 0, SEQ[0], ENDDELAY 0, SEQ[1], ENDDELAY 1 play in turn, starting from whichever SEQSTART was triggered and always ending after delay 1, LOOP.CNT times, then LOOPSDONE; REFRESH and ENDDELAY are ignored at that end since the last value is held. Only SEQ[1] can raise LOOPSDONE, which needs LOOP > 0 and SEQ[1].CNT > 0 at start. A single sequence repeats until stopped when placed in SEQ[1] with LOOP = 1 and the LOOPSDONE to SEQSTART1 shortcut on. If the period is shorter than the time EasyDMA needs to fetch and load a value, the previous compare value repeats.

OUT[0] to OUT[3] go to the pins in PSEL.OUT[n]; with CONNECT set to Disconnected the signal reaches no pin. The settings apply while PWM is enabled and generating and are kept only in System ON. The pins should be set in GPIO as outputs, their GPIO OUT value giving the idle level, before PWM is enabled, and kept so for as long as the external circuit is attached, so they stay defined after a STOP, while PWM is disabled or in System OFF. Only one peripheral may drive a given pin.

The quadrature decoder reads two-phase signals from mechanical or optical incremental encoders, sampling at a set period and accumulating the result so the application need not keep up in real time. It has optional debounce filters and an optional LED output for optical encoders. The application core has QDEC0 and QDEC1.

Phases A and B are 90 degrees apart, and which one changes first gives the direction; both changing in one sample is invalid, which happens if the encoder turns too fast for the sample rate. The inputs are sampled every SAMPLEPER and each sample pair is compared with the previous one. SAMPLEPER may only be changed between STOP (after STOPPED) and START; LEDPOL, REPORTPER, DBFEN and LEDPRE are best changed only while stopped.

The LED output follows the sample period: it turns on LEDPRE before each sample and off right after. LEDPOL sets its polarity, and setting PSEL.LED CONNECT to Disconnected frees the pin for encoders that need no LED. With DBFEN on, each phase input is sampled at 1 MHz through the whole sample period and passes only if every sample agrees: a level steady for longer than twice SAMPLEPER always passes and one shorter than SAMPLEPER never does, the input being assumed below 500 kHz. With the filters on the LED stays on, since sampling is continuous, and reported motion is delayed by one SAMPLEPER.

ACC sums the valid samples (+1 and -1), giving the movement since it was last cleared; double transitions (2) are not added. A sample that would overflow or underflow ACC is dropped and raises ACCOF. ACCDBL counts double transitions since its last clearing. READCLRACC copies both to ACCREAD and ACCDBLREAD and clears them; RDCLRACC and RDCLRDBL do the same for one each. REPORTPER sets how many samples are gathered before evaluation: REPORTRDY follows if the movement is not zero, DBLRDY if double transitions were seen. The shortcuts DBLRDY_RDCLRACC and DBLRDY_RDCLRDBL can trigger the read-and-clear tasks.

Phase A, Phase B and LED go to the pins in PSEL.A, PSEL.B and PSEL.LED, taken when ENABLE is set; the CPU can read but not write them then. A signal set to Disconnected reaches no pin. The settings apply only while QDEC is enabled and are kept only in System ON; when disabled the pins act as plain GPIO with their OUT and PIN_CNF settings. The pins should be set up in GPIO before QDEC is enabled and kept so while it is. Only one peripheral may drive a given pin.

QSPI talks to an external flash over single, dual or quad SPI with a clock from 6 to 96 MHz. It offers single-word reads and writes, EasyDMA block transfers reading at up to 48 MB/s, execute-in-place (XIP) from the external flash (which can be turned off), and on-the-fly encryption and decryption for both EasyDMA and XIP.

Choose the pins in PSEL.SCK, PSEL.CSN and PSEL.IO0 to PSEL.IO3, using only the dedicated QSPI pins; set those pins to high drive; give them to the peripheral through the GPIO dedicated-peripheral setting; configure the flash interface in IFCONFIG0, IFCONFIG1 and ADDRCONF; enable QSPI with ENABLE, which takes the pins; then trigger ACTIVATE, after which READY shows the flash is ready. If IFCONFIG0 selects quad mode, the flash itself must also be put in quad mode, by custom instruction, before transfers.

A write is set up in WRITE.DST, WRITE.SRC and WRITE.CNT and started by WRITESTART; QSPI splits it into page writes, and READY marks the end. A read uses READ.SRC, READ.DST and READ.CNT with READSTART, and READY marks the end. An erase of pages or blocks uses ERASE.PTR and ERASE.LEN with ERASESTART; for an erase READY only means the erase has begun, and whether it has finished is normally learned by querying the flash with a custom instruction.
Once the flash is configured, the CPU can run code from it through the XIP memory region, which is read-only (a write gives a bus error). The start of the XIP region maps to flash address XIPOFFSET.

A stream cipher between the AHB bus and the flash can protect its contents, XIP and EasyDMA each having their own enable, key and nonce. AES-128 turns the key, the nonce and the flash address into a keystream that is combined with each 32-bit data word. The same key and nonce must be used to encrypt and decrypt a given address. The address is the flash address, independent of XIPOFFSET, so a second image can be written encrypted by EasyDMA and then run by pointing XIPOFFSET at it. Encryption and decryption are the same operation, so plain-text flash read with the cipher on reaches the MCU scrambled. For XIP: write XIP_ENC.KEY0 to KEY3 and XIP_ENC.NONCE0 to NONCE2, then set XIP_ENC.ENABLE. For EasyDMA: the same with the DMA_ENC registers. Custom instruction data is not encrypted.

A custom instruction is a one-byte opcode with up to 8 bytes of data, and its response can be read. Data goes in CINSTRDAT0 and CINSTRDAT1 first; writing the opcode and settings to CINSTRCONF sends it, always on a single data line.
