READY follows, and CINSTRDAT0 and CINSTRDAT1 then hold the response. Long frame mode (LFEN and LFSTOP in CINSTRCONF) allows any length: every CINSTRCONF write carries LFEN = 1; the opcode goes only with the first, each later write sends LENGTH - 1 data bytes, LIO2 and LIO3 are set by the first write for the whole frame, and the last write sets LFSTOP = 1.

The flash can be put into deep power-down mode when not needed. It is enabled in IFCONFIG0, timed by DPMDUR (set from the flash's specification so that STATUS and the READY timing are right), entered and left through IFCONFIG1, and its state is read in STATUS.
IFTIMING.RXDELAY (0 to 7, reset value 2) sets how many prescaled 192 MHz cycles after the rising SCK edge the input data is sampled; 0 samples on the rising edge itself.

The network core's 2.4 GHz transceiver supports Bluetooth LE at 1 and 2 Mbps and Long Range at 125 and 500 kbps, Bluetooth LE direction finding (AoA and AoD), IEEE 802.15.4 at 250 kbps, and Nordic proprietary modes at 1 and 2 Mbps. EasyDMA with a hardware packet assembler and disassembler and CRC generation and checking moves packets to and from RAM. It also filters addresses and matches patterns, checks device addresses on the fly and times the gap between frames (for Bluetooth LE whitelisting and spacing), measures RSSI, and a bit counter that raises events after a set number of bits sent or received.

A packet holds PREAMBLE, ADDRESS (base address then prefix), S0, LENGTH, S1, PAYLOAD and CRC, sent in that order; Long Range Bluetooth LE adds CI and TERM1 after the address and TERM2 after the CRC. A static payload add-on of PCNF1.STATLEN bytes (0 in a standard BLE packet) goes between PAYLOAD and CRC. In RAM a packet is stored as S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD only; PREAMBLE, ADDRESS, CI, TERM1, TERM2 and CRC are left out, and S0, LENGTH and S1 are optional. ADDRESS and PAYLOAD go least significant byte first and CRC most significant byte first; ADDRESS bits go LSB first and CRC bits MSB first, while PCNF1.ENDIAN sets bit order for S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD. S0LEN, LFLEN and S1LEN in PCNF0 size those fields; below 8 bits their least significant bits are used, a zero-length field is absent from RAM, and any other takes its own byte. S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD together cannot exceed 258 bytes, whatever PCNF1.MAXLEN says.

The on-air ADDRESS is a base address plus a prefix byte. PCNF1.BALEN sets the base length; below 4 bytes the base is cut from its least significant byte. On-air addresses are written only in BASE0, BASE1, PREFIX0 and PREFIX1; TXADDRESS, RXADDRESSES and RXMATCH use logical addresses 0 to 7.

With PCNF1.WHITEEN set, packets are whitened and de-whitened automatically over everything but the preamble and address, using a whitening word from the polynomial g(D) = D7 + D4 + 1 XORed with the data; DATAWHITEIV seeds the shift register. Whitened packets cannot include the address in the CRC (CRCCNF.SKIPADDR=Include). The CRC covers the whole packet except the preamble, and optionally the address too (CRCCNF). Its polynomial is set in CRCPOLY (bit 0 is X0), its length in CRCCNF and its starting value in CRCINIT; the packet is clocked through serially. The running CRC cannot be read, but a received one can, in RXCRC. After a full packet, CRCOK or CRCERROR follows and CRCSTATUS holds the result.

TXEN or RXEN starts a ramp-up (TXRU or RXRU); READY marks arrival in TXIDLE or RXIDLE, and only then may START begin a packet. ADDRESS, PAYLOAD (raised even for a zero-length payload), END (packet done) and PHYEND (last bit on air) follow; STOP returns to idle and DISABLE leads through TXDISABLE or RXDISABLE to DISABLED. RADIO does not block a task given in the wrong state, which may then misbehave. In IEEE 802.15.4 and Long Range modes the PHYEND to START shortcut should be used instead of END to START.

Without shortcuts the CPU's own response time separates READY from START and END from DISABLE; during those gaps the transmitter sends 1s by default (MODECNF0.DTX sets what is sent), and the receiver listens from START, taking in undefined data until a valid preamble. Shortcuts READY to START and END to DISABLE remove the gaps. Several packets can be sent or received one after another without disabling between them.

RSSI is measured continuously through a single-pole IIR filter and settles about RSSISETTLE after a level change. RSSISTART starts sampling and RSSISAMPLE holds the filtered value after RSSIPERIOD. It is valid only with RADIO enabled in RX (RXEN) and reception started (READY, then START).

IFS is the time from the end of the last received bit to the start of the first transmitted bit of the next packet. RADIO holds it to TIFS as long as TIFS is not shorter than its turnaround time; TIFS runs from the last bit on air (just before END) to the first bit sent (just after READY). RADIO enforces it only when END is shortcut to DISABLE and DISABLED is shortcut to TXEN (or to RXEN). TIFS is qualified for IEEE 802.15.4 250 kbps, Bluetooth LE Long Range, and Bluetooth LE 1 and 2 Mbps with the default ramp-up. SHORTS and TIFS are not double-buffered and may be changed until the last bit is received; MODE is double-buffered and sampled at TXEN or RXEN.

For Bluetooth LE whitelisting, RADIO can match device addresses on the fly while receiving, in little-endian configuration only. It takes the first 48 payload bits as the device address and bit 6 of S0 as TxAdd. Eight addresses can be watched at once, each a DAB register (low 32 bits) and DAP register (high 16 bits) with a TxAdd bit in DACNF, where each can also be included or excluded.

BCSTART starts the counter, only after the ADDRESS event, and BCMATCH is raised when it reaches BCC; it keeps counting until DISABLED or BCSTOP, and BCC can be rewritten after each BCMATCH for further matches in the same packet. BCSTOP, STOP, DISABLE or END stop and reset it. Shortcuts can start it from RADIO events.

In Bluetooth LE 1 and 2 Mbps modes RADIO supports AoA and AoD. The transmitter appends a constant tone extension (CTE) after the CRC, and the receiver takes IQ samples during it while an antenna array at the transmitter (AoD) or receiver (AoA) is switched between antennas; the phase differences give the direction. The CTE lasts 16 µs to 160 µs and is an unwhitened run of 1s, a tone about +250 kHz from the carrier at 1 Mbps and +500 kHz at 2 Mbps. It has a 4 µs guard period, an 8 µs reference period, then alternating switch and sample slots of 1 or 2 µs (both the same). Antennas switch in switch slots and the guard period; one IQ sample is needed per microsecond of the reference period and one per sample slot, and oversampling is possible. CTE format, switching and sampling can be set before or during a packet, or in RX taken from the packet itself.

With CTEINLINECONF.CTEINLINECTRLEN set, RX takes the CTE settings from the packet's CP bit and CTEInfo octet (present only when CP is set). A Data Channel PDU (CTEINFOINS1=InS1) needs LFLEN of 8 bits and an S0LEN of 1 byte; S1 is taken as present when S0 AND S0MASK equals S0CONF, and then the CP bit, not S1LEN, decides its size (0 or 8 bits). With CCM encryption, PCNF0.S1INCL must be 1 and CCM must use an 8-bit length field; CP enters the MIC while S1 does not. For Advertising Channel PDUs (NotInS1) the CTEInfo flag in the extended header flags plays the part of CP (in AUX_SYNC_IND and AUX_CHAIN_IND, for instance); S0CONF and S0MASK can restrict the accepted PDU types; with a non-zero extended header length the flag is checked, and any flag set before it moves CTEInfo 6 octets later. CTEInfo holds CTETime (5 bits, CTE length in 8 µs units), an RFU bit and CTEType (2 bits). CTETIMEVALIDRANGE sets the upper valid CTETime, optionally using the RFU bit; CTETime of 0 or 1 is taken as the 16 µs minimum. CTEType sets the slot length and so which RX sample spacing applies.

Without inline configuration the packet is not parsed: DFECTRL1.NUMBEROF8US gives the CTE length in 8 µs units, DFECTRL1.DFEINEXTENSION makes the procedure start from the end of the CRC or from the ADDRESS event, and DFECTRL2.TSWITCHOFFSET and DFECTRL2.TSAMPLEOFFSET add offsets for switching and sampling. A transmitted packet carries the CTE after its CRC; a received CTE raises CTEPRESENT.

RADIO can drive up to 8 GPIOs to switch external antennas, chosen in PSEL.DFEGPIO[n]; only pins marked Connected are driven. In AoD TX and AoA RX it takes the pins while it needs them and otherwise leaves them to their GPIO settings, so they must be configured in GPIO. The switch patterns are written one after another into SWITCHPATTERN: the first applies from TXEN or RXEN until the first switch, the second to the reference period from the start of the guard period, and the rest to each switch slot in turn; past the end the sequence wraps to SWITCHPATTERN[2]. When the procedure ends, SWITCHPATTERN[0] is applied DFECTRL1.TSWITCHSPACING after the last switch. At least three patterns must be written; CLEARPATTERN empties the buffer. Without inline configuration, DFECTRL1.TSWITCHSPACING sets switch spacing and DFECTRL2.TSWITCHOFFSET the first switch's position.

IQ samples taken during the CTE, relative to the RX carrier, are written by DMA to DFEPACKET.PTR, up to DFEPACKET.MAXCNT, with the count in DFEPACKET.AMOUNT; DFECTRL1.SAMPLETYPE can store magnitude and phase instead. In the reference period DFECTRL1.TSAMPLESPACINGREF sets the spacing, and DFECTRL2.TSAMPLEOFFSET shifts samples in 16 MHz steps (62.5 ns). After it, DFECTRL1.TSAMPLESPACING sets the spacing unless inline configuration is on, in which case it is set by CTEType (AoD RX) or by DFECTRL1.TSWITCHSPACING (AoA RX), as in the inline sample-spacing tables. TSAMPLESPACINGREF and TSAMPLESPACING allow oversampling.

MODE=Ieee802154_250kbit implements the IEEE 802.15.4-2006 250 kbps O-QPSK PHY at 2450 MHz, with clear channel assessment, energy detection scan and CRC generation. A frame is a 5-octet synchronization header (four zero preamble octets, 160 µs, and the start of frame delimiter 0xA7, 32 µs with the PHR), a 1-octet PHY header and up to 127 octets of PSDU (up to 4064 µs), of which 125 are usable with CRC. A symbol lasts 16 µs. The SFD register can set a non-standard SFD for basic frame filtering. RADIO itself produces the preamble and SFD; software does not put them in the buffer. The PHR's low 7 bits give the PSDU length and its top bit is reserved (0 when compliant) but reported; the PHR is the first byte at PACKETPTR. Zero-length frames are discarded without FRAMESTART. A MAC frame is N-2 octets of PHY data, the last two being the CRC: frame control field (2 octets), sequence number (1), addressing fields (0 to 20), payload, and a 16-bit FCS (ITU-T CRC over header and payload) generated on transmit and checked into CRCSTATUS on receive.

Energy detection samples received power in the channel to find activity. The READY to START shortcut should be off before entering RX so the signal is not decoded. RSSI samples are averaged over 8 symbols (128 µs). The standard asks for a value from 0 to 255, 0 meaning less than 10 dB above sensitivity, spanning at least 40 dB linearly within ±6 dB. EDSTART starts a measurement and EDEND ends it; EDSAMPLE × ED_RSSISCALE, capped at 255, gives the IEEE scale. With EDCNT not 0, the measurement repeats EDCNT+1 times (128 × N µs for EDCNT = N-1) and EDSAMPLE keeps the maximum, which cuts interrupts and power during channel scans. EDSTOP stops it, followed by EDSTOPPED.

CCA checks whether the medium is busy for CSMA-CA, over 8 symbols (128 µs), with RADIO in RX and able to receive; the READY to START shortcut should be off if no baseband processing is wanted meanwhile. Mode 1 (CCAMODE=EdMode) compares an ED measurement with CCACTRL.CCAEDTHRES: at or above it gives CCABUSY, below it CCAIDLE. Mode 2 (CarrierMode) reports busy if a valid SFD is seen, or a frame is being received; with CCACORRCNT not zero, busy is also reported once more than CCACORRCNT correlator peaks exceed CCACORRTHRES; otherwise CCAIDLE. Mode 3 (CarrierAndEdMode or CarrierOrEdMode) ANDs or ORs the two. EDSAMPLE is updated at the end, holding the first ED measurement for EdModeTest1 and the average otherwise. CCASTOP ends a CCA, followed by CCASTOPPED. Shortcuts: CCAIDLE to TXEN with CCAIDLE to STOP moves straight to transmit, CCABUSY to DISABLE turns RADIO off on a busy channel, and RXREADY to CCASTART starts a CCA as soon as RX is ready.

The FCS is a 16-bit ITU-T CRC, G(x) = x16 + x12 + x5 + 1, over the MAC header and payload, started at 0. In RX it begins with the first octet after the PHR and updates each octet; on a full frame CRCSTATUS is set and CRCOK or CRCERROR raised, and the two CRC octets are not written to RAM. In TX it is computed on the fly from the first octet after the PHR and inserted as the last two octets, EasyDMA fetching length minus 2 octets. Set CRCCNF to a 16-bit CRC with SKIPADDR=Ieee802154, CRCPOLY = 0x11021 and CRCINIT = 0; little-endian ordering is needed because the FCS is sent left bit first.

Transmit starts in RX: RXEN, then on READY a CCASTART; CCAIDLE or CCABUSY follows 128 µs later. On busy, retry after the standard's CSMA-CA back-off. On idle, TXEN ramps up to TXIDLE and READY; with PACKETPTR on the PHR, START sends the four-octet preamble, the SFD, then the PHR and that many bytes, the CRC (if on) covering PHR-2 octets and filling the last two; CRC parameters are sampled at START and the FCS is little-endian. Shortcuts READY to CCASTART and CCAIDLE to TXEN automate this. Receive: RXEN, READY in RXIDLE, then START enables baseband processing. After a valid SHR, octets from the PHR on are stored at PACKETPTR, FRAMESTART follows the SFD, the CRC runs from the first payload byte over the whole frame (its two bytes not stored), CRCOK follows a zero result, and END comes when the last octet is in memory. An LQI byte is appended after the last stored octet (after the MSDU for a compliant frame); it is the median of three RSSI readings taken during the frame, valid for frames of at least three octets, and converts to the IEEE range when multiplied by 4 with the result held to 8 bits (saturating). A FRAMESTART to BCSTART shortcut can raise BCMATCH after N bits, for example to inspect the address fields.

IFS gives the MAC time to process a frame and must separate frames, after the acknowledgement where one is requested. It is macMinSIFSPeriod (12 symbols) for an MPDU up to aMaxSIFSFrameSize (18 octets) and macMinLIFSPeriod (40 symbols) for longer ones; the acknowledgement turnaround tack is 32 symbols. The assisted modes set TIFS to suit each frame; otherwise TIFS must be updated by software.

One double-buffered PACKETPTR serves both RX and TX and should be set before each START. END marks the last bit processed and DISABLED the completion of DISABLE. RAM holds S0, LENGTH, S1 and PAYLOAD, with the static add-on sent straight after the payload; each field is padded to whole bytes (3 bits take 1 byte, 9 bits 2 bytes), and any may be zero length if the protocol allows. CI, TERM1 and TERM2 exist only in Long Range mode. PCNF1.MAXLEN caps payload plus add-on (not S0, LENGTH or S1) in bytes so RADIO stays within its buffer: a longer payload is truncated to MAXLEN, its LENGTH field is left unchanged and the CRC is computed as if the length were MAXLEN. A PACKETPTR outside Data RAM can cause a HardFault or RAM corruption.

The random number generator makes true random numbers from internal thermal noise, fit for cryptographic use, and needs no seed. START begins generation and STOP ends it. While running, each new byte is written to VALUE and a VALRDY event is raised; the byte must be read before the next VALRDY, when it is overwritten. The RNG is a network core peripheral.

An optional bias correction step, enabled in CONFIG, removes any lean toward 1 or 0 in the raw bit stream before the bits are packed eight at a time into VALUE. It makes the output statistically uniform but slows generation. The time to produce a byte varies from byte to byte and cannot be predicted, more so with bias correction on.

The real-time counter is a low-power timer clocked from LFCLK: a 24-bit COUNTER behind a 12-bit prescaler, capture/compare registers CC[n] and a TICK event generator. Starting the RTC requests LFCLK from the RC oscillator if LFCLK is not already running. The application core has RTC0 and RTC1, and the network core has its own RTC0 and RTC1; each has four CC registers (CC[0..3]).

PRESCALER can be written only while the RTC is stopped. Its value is latched into the internal prescaler on the START, CLEAR and TRIGOVRFLW tasks. The internal counter steps on an LFCLK edge whenever the internal prescaler has counted down to zero, after which the prescaler reloads; each step gives a TICK event when TICK is enabled.

Reading COUNTER samples the internal counter safely across the LFCLK boundary by stalling the CPU and memory bus for four PCLK16M cycles; with the two cycles of the read itself a COUNTER read takes at most six PCLK16M cycles.

OVRFLW is raised when COUNTER wraps from 0xFFFFFF to 0. The TRIGOVRFLW task sets COUNTER to 0xFFFFF0 so the overflow can be tested in software. TICK gives a regular interrupt for a tickless RTOS without SysTick, so the CPU can power down while scheduling continues. OVRFLW and TICK are both disabled by default.

Each RTC event can be disabled individually in EVTEN so that it does not request PCLK16M and HFCLK, saving power. An event reaches DPPI only when enabled in EVTEN, and the CPU interrupt only when enabled in INTEN, so the RTC's task and event scheme differs slightly from the standard peripheral interface.

Each CC register has a CAPTURE task that copies the internal counter into CC[n]; CC[n] is updated 6 PCLK16M periods after the task. When CAPTURE and CLEAR arrive together, CAPTURE wins and CC[n] holds the value before the reset. A CAPTURE never raises the matching COMPARE event even though CC[n] then equals COUNTER.

COMPARE[n] is raised when COUNTER steps from N-1 to a CC[n] value of N. A CC of 0 at a CLEAR task gives no event, and a CC equal to COUNTER when START is triggered gives no event. With COUNTER at N, writing N+2 to CC is sure to give an event at N+2, while writing N or N+1 may not. Replacing a CC that holds N+1 or N+2 can still give an event on that old value before the new one applies; an old value above N+2 cannot fire. With the COMPARE[i]_CLEAR short enabled, COUNTER clears one LFCLK cycle after the COMPARE event.

The CPU-side registers are in the PCLK16M domain and mirror registers in the LFCLK domain, so tasks wait on LFCLK edges. CLEAR, STOP and TRIGOVRFLW take effect after the RTC sees one falling and one rising LFCLK edge, between 15.2585 μs and 45.7755 μs later (about 15 μs to 46 μs). After STOP no further events are raised, but COUNTER may still step once more. With LFCLK already running and stable, the first COUNTER step and TICK after START come typically 30.5 μs ±15 μs later; if LFCLK is not yet running, its start-up time adds to this, and the same applies to TRIGOVRFLW. Software that must know the RTC is running waits for the first TICK. Jitter of the 32.768 kHz clock adds to the RTC task and event jitter.

The SAADC is a differential successive-approximation ADC with 8, 10 or 12-bit resolution, and 14 bits with oversampling. Up to eight channels each pick any of AIN0 to AIN7, VDD, or VDDHDIV5 (VDDH divided by 5): one channel per single-ended input, two per differential input, and single-ended and differential channels can be mixed in a scan. Full-scale input range is 0 to VDD. Sampling is started by a task from software or through PPI (for example from the 32.768 kHz RTC or a 1/16 MHz TIMER), or by its own timer for continuous sampling. It offers one-shot and scan modes with configurable sample delay, EasyDMA transfer of results to RAM, interrupts per sample and on a full buffer, results as 16-bit two's complement for both single-ended and differential inputs, an internal resistor string, and on-the-fly limit checking. It is an application core peripheral.

The SAADC and COMP can be used together on AIN0 to AIN7 as long as they use different pins; the same analog pin should not be selected for both. A channel selected for COMP cannot be sampled by the SAADC at the same time.

The converter is always differential inside. In single-ended mode (CH[n].CONFIG.MODE = SE, the default) the negative input is tied to ground internally, so the ADC's internal ground is taken as the reference of the measured voltage and the result is sensitive to ground bounce on the board. Differential mode (MODE = Diff) reduces this.

Results deviate from the ideal through DC errors (offset, gain, DNL, INL), which matter most for battery measurement, and AC errors (gain stage non-linearity, settling with a high source impedance, sampling jitter). With REFSEL = 0 the core's nominal input range is ±0.6 V differential and the gain must scale the input to fit. The offset drifts with temperature, so over a wide temperature range CALIBRATEOFFSET should be run at regular intervals; CALIBRATEDONE, DONE and RESULTDONE are raised when calibration finishes.

Up to eight channels CH[0..7] can be set up. Setting CH[n].PSELP selects the positive input and enables the channel; CH[n].PSELN selects the negative input and is used only when that channel is in differential mode. One enabled channel gives one-shot operation; more than one enabled channel puts the ADC in scan mode.

STATUS shows a conversion in progress and toggles at the end of each conversion during scan, oversampling and continuous operation. Scan mode and oversampling cannot be combined. In one-shot mode a SAMPLE task takes one sample with the acquisition time set by CH[n].CONFIG.TACQ, and DONE marks it. Continuous sampling uses the ADC's own timer (SAMPLERATE.MODE = Timers: one SAMPLE task starts it, STOP ends it, SAMPLERATE.CC sets the rate; one channel only and not with scan) or a general-purpose TIMER triggering SAMPLE through PPI. Without oversampling, RESULTDONE means the same as DONE. DONE and RESULTDONE can come before EasyDMA has written the value to RAM.

An accumulator averages 2^OVERSAMPLE samples (OVERSAMPLE register) into one result before it is written to RAM, improving SNR but not INL or DNL; it should not be combined with scan, since it would average across channels. The SAMPLE task must occur 2^OVERSAMPLE times, from the local or a general-purpose timer, from software, or by setting CH[n].CONFIG.BURST, which takes all the samples as fast as possible (in less than (tACQ + tCONV) × 2^OVERSAMPLE) so that it behaves like one longer one-shot conversion. DONE marks each sample and RESULTDONE marks an oversampled result ready for RAM.

Results are packed two 16-bit values per 32-bit RAM word, in channel order across successive scans: with channels 1, 2 and 5 enabled the buffer holds CH1, CH2, CH5, CH1, CH2, CH5 and so on. With an odd RESULT.MAXCNT the last word holds a single result.

After RESULT.PTR and RESULT.MAXCNT are set, START starts the ADC and EasyDMA writes results to the buffer at RESULT.PTR, little-endian and sign-extended to 16 bits. RESULT.PTR is double-buffered and can be loaded for the next START as soon as STARTED is raised. END is raised when RESULT.MAXCNT results have been written; START must then be triggered again before more samples are taken. STOP ends any sampling in progress and gives STOPPED, also when already stopped. EasyDMA is done with RAM once END or STOPPED is raised, and RESULT.AMOUNT then tells how many results were written since START. A RESULT.PTR outside RAM the peripheral can reach may give a HardFault or corrupt memory. In scan mode RESULT.MAXCNT should be at least the number of enabled channels.
An internal resistor string on each of the positive and negative inputs can pull the input up or down, set by CH[n].CONFIG.RESP and RESN.

CH[n].CONFIG.REFSEL picks the internal reference, which gives a core input range of ±0.6 V, or VDD, which gives ±VDD/4. The gain stage scales the effective input range. AIN0 to AIN7 must stay between VSS and VDD.
The ADC samples by connecting a capacitor to the input for the acquisition time set in CH[n].CONFIG.TACQ; a higher source resistance needs a longer time. VDDHDIV5 needs at least 10 µs.

Each channel compares its results against CH[n].LIMIT: a result above the high limit raises CH[n].LIMITH and one below the low limit raises CH[n].LIMITL. LIMIT.HIGH must be greater than or equal to LIMIT.LOW, so only results outside the window give events; swapping the limits does not give an inside-the-window event. The comparison always runs and needs no enable; unused events are simply ignored.

Sample-timing jitter (between START tasks, or from START to acquisition, including timer accuracy and regulator and reference start-up) and circuit noise from CPU activity and the DC/DC regulator degrade ADC results. The best results come with START timed by a TIMER, the HFXO as clock source, and constant latency mode.

The SPI master with EasyDMA talks to several slaves, each with its own chip select. It supports SPI modes 0 to 3, moves data to and from RAM by EasyDMA, lets every signal use any pin, and can drive an optional D/CX line that marks command and data bytes.

START begins a transaction that clocks bytes out on MOSI and in on MISO. ENDTX is raised when all TXD.MAXCNT bytes of the transmit buffer have been sent and ENDRX when RXD.MAXCNT bytes have been received; END follows once both have occurred, and the transaction then stops by itself. When more bytes are to be received than sent, the ORC byte is sent after the transmit buffer runs out; when more are sent than received, the extra received bytes are discarded. STOP finishes the byte in progress and then gives STOPPED (also when idle); ENDTX and ENDRX are raised on stopping if they have not been already. SUSPEND pauses after the current byte and RESUME continues.

For slaves such as display drivers that need a command/data line, SPIM drives D/CX low while command bytes are sent and high for data bytes. PSELDCX picks the pin and DCXCNT (0x0 to 0xF) gives the number of command bytes before the data bytes; 0xF makes every byte a command byte. DCXCNT must not be written during a transfer.

SCK, CSN, DCX, MOSI and MISO go to the pins named in the PSEL registers, which can be written only while SPIM is disabled, are used only while it is enabled and are kept only in System ON. The pins must be set up in GPIO as in the SPIM GPIO configuration, with the dedicated peripheral setting selected, before SPIM is enabled, and only one peripheral may drive a pin. Some SPIM instances have no automatic CSN control, and CSN is then driven as a GPIO. CONFIG sets CPOL and CPHA.

Peripherals with the same ID as SPIM share its registers and other resources, so all of them must be disabled before SPIM is configured. Disabling them does not reset the shared registers, so every SPIM register in use must be written explicitly.

Both pointer and count registers are double-buffered, so the next transfer can be set up once STARTED is raised. ENDTX and ENDRX mean EasyDMA has finished with the TX or RX buffer, and END that both are finished. How a channel behaves under AHB bus congestion, when several masters reach for the same slave, depends on the SPIM instance.
For the lowest current when SPIM is not needed, stop and disable it. If STOP is sent, wait for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE.

The SPI slave with EasyDMA serves an external SPI master at very low power. EasyDMA and a hardware semaphore remove any real-time demand on the CPU, which can manage the slave from a low-priority context. It supports SPI modes 0 to 3, set by CPOL and CPHA in CONFIG.

Peripherals with the same ID as SPIS share its registers and other resources, so all of them must be disabled before SPIS is configured, and since disabling them resets nothing, every SPIS register in use must be written explicitly.

SPIS works from two RAM buffers at RXD.PTR and TXD.PTR, shared with the CPU under a hardware semaphore. The CPU triggers ACQUIRE and waits for ACQUIRED before changing the pointers, then triggers RELEASE so that SPIS can take the semaphore (RELEASE does nothing if the CPU does not hold it). If the pointers are not changed between granted transactions, the same TX data goes out again and the RX buffer is overwritten; the END_ACQUIRE short hands the semaphore back to the CPU after every granted transaction to allow an update. ENDRX is raised when the RX buffer is full. Bytes received beyond RXD.MAXCNT are discarded and flagged as OVERFLOW in STATUS; bytes clocked out beyond TXD.MAXCNT are the ORC character and flagged as OVERREAD. When more is received than sent, the remainder sent is ORC. RXD.AMOUNT and TXD.AMOUNT are updated at the end of each granted transaction with the bytes written to RX and read from TX (ORC bytes not counted). END means EasyDMA has finished with the buffer.

After SPIS is enabled the semaphore belongs to the CPU, with no ACQUIRED event for that first handover; ACQUIRE while the CPU holds it gives ACQUIRED at once. When CSN falls (STARTED), SPIS tries to take the semaphore. If the CPU holds it, the transaction is ignored: MOSI data is discarded and the DEF character is sent on MISO for the whole transaction, even if the CPU releases it part way through. If both ask at the same moment, the CPU gets it. If SPIS gets it, the transaction is granted: MOSI data goes to the RX buffer and the TX buffer goes out on MISO. When CSN rises after a granted transaction SPIS releases the semaphore and raises END, and it can be granted transaction after transaction while the semaphore is free. An ACQUIRE from the CPU during a granted transaction is served once SPIS releases the semaphore; with END_ACQUIRE enabled only one such ACQUIRE is served after END. The semaphore never blocks CPU access to the pointers or the RAM; it only says when changing them is safe. A master can use the DEF character to end an ungranted transaction early.

Each of the four signals goes to the pin named in its own PSEL register; CONNECT = Disconnected leaves a signal unconnected. These registers are written only while SPIS is disabled, used only while it is enabled and kept only in System ON; when disabled the pins act as ordinary GPIOs from OUT and PIN_CNF[n]. The SPIS GPIO configuration must be made before enabling SPIS and kept as long as an external master is to see the slave, so the pins stay correct while SPIS is briefly disabled or the device is in System OFF. MISO is high impedance while CSN does not select the slave. Only one peripheral may drive a pin.

The system protection unit is the one place that sets access rights to memories, peripherals and other resources. It supports Arm TrustZone with memory regions that are secure, non-secure, or callable from non-secure code; extends that protection to masters other than the CPU, such as EasyDMA; keeps non-secure code and peripherals off secure pins; stops non-secure peripherals publishing to or subscribing from secure DPPI channels; and controls access from the other cores' domains. The SPU is an application core peripheral, always secure.

For RAM, flash and peripherals, SPU-controlled logic checks the address and attributes (read, write, execute, secure) of every bus transfer and blocks it if needed. For a CPU master the decision rests on the CPU's security state and the security state SPU reports for the address; for any other master, on that master's security attribute set in an SPU register. Blocked reads return zero and blocked writes are ignored (RAZ/WI). A security violation by a Cortex-M33 gives a SecureFault; other violations give an SPU event, which can interrupt the CPU. For pins and DPPI channels, the resource's security attribute is checked against the attribute of the peripheral that wants it; SPU alone sets those attributes.

SPU drives the Cortex-M33's implementation-defined attribution unit (IDAU), giving full support for TrustZone instructions such as test target (TT) and for non-secure callable regions as secure entry points. To use SPU, the core's SAU must be disabled with all memory marked non-secure, so that SPU sets the security attribution through the IDAU.

Flash is divided into 64 regions of 16 KiB. Each region has its own read (data reads; code fetch is governed by execute), write (writes and page erase), execute (code fetch, even with read off) and secure (only secure transfers) permissions, set independently and lockable until reset with FLASHREGION[n].PERM.LOCK. A debugger can step through execute-protected regions.

operation.topic: SPU non-secure callable regions in flash
operation.text: A non-secure callable sub-region lets non-secure code call into secure code. It lies inside a secure region chosen by FLASHNSC[n].REGION, has a size set by FLASHNSC[n].SIZE (a SIZE value m gives 2^(m+4) bytes), and runs down from the top address of that region. It exists only when SIZE is non-zero and the chosen region is secure; if the chosen region is non-secure there is no NSC sub-region and the region stays non-secure. Two FLASHNSC entries naming the same region give one sub-region of the larger size.

On a flash access violation the transfer is blocked, a read returns zero, and the master gets a bus error where it supports one. A CPU security violation gives a SecureFault; a CPU read, write or execute violation gives a BusFault. FLASHACCERR is raised for every violation except a CPU security violation, and can interrupt the CPU. A SecureFault takes precedence over a BusFault when both arise together.

UICR and FICR are always secure. FICR is read-only; UICR is read and written by secure code only, using the NVMC procedure. Code fetched from UICR or FICR counts as a violation, debug sessions excepted.

RAM is split into 64 regions of 8 KiB apiece, each having independent read, write, execute and secure permissions, lockable until reset with RAMREGION[n].PERM.LOCK. Non-secure callable sub-regions are set with RAMNSC[n].REGION and RAMNSC[n].SIZE under the same rules as in flash (2^(m+4) bytes, from the top of a secure region down).

On a RAM access violation the transfer is blocked, a read returns zero and the master gets a bus error where it supports one. A Cortex-M33 security violation gives a SecureFault, and a Cortex-M33 read, write or execute violation a BusFault. RAMACCERR is raised for every violation except a Cortex-M33 security violation. A SecureFault takes precedence over a BusFault when both arise together.

A peripheral's security attribute is always secure (system control peripherals), always non-secure (some general-purpose peripherals) or configurable to secure-only; PERIPHID[n].PERM shows which, and sets it where it is not fixed. At reset every user-selectable and split-security peripheral is secure, with secure DMA where it has DMA. Secure code can reach both secure and non-secure peripherals. A split-security peripheral serves secure and non-secure code on one resource: set non-secure, some of its registers and bit fields are reachable only by secure transfers; set secure, only secure transfers reach it at all.

Non-secure peripherals sit at 0x4XXXXXXX and secure ones at 0x5XXXXXXX; a user-selectable peripheral appears at one or the other according to its attribute. Reaching a secure peripheral at 0x4XXXXXXX gives a bus error whatever the CPU's state, and so does secure code reaching a non-secure peripheral at 0x5XXXXXXX. A split-security peripheral set non-secure appears at 0x4XXXXXXX for non-secure access, where its secure registers read as zero and ignore writes, and at 0x5XXXXXXX, where secure code reaches both kinds of register; set secure it appears only at 0x5XXXXXXX. Any access from non-secure code to 0x50000000 to 0x5FFFFFFF is ignored and gives a SecureFault.

operation.topic: SPU peripherals with a DMA master
operation.text: A peripheral with DMA can make its DMA transfers with a different security attribute from its own, so a secure peripheral can move non-secure data. This needs the DMA field of PERIPHID[n].PERM to read SeparateAttribute and the peripheral to be secure (SECATTR = 1); DMASEC then picks Secure or NonSecure for its transfers.

On a peripheral access violation the transfer is blocked, a read returns zero, the master gets a bus error where it supports one (a TrustZone processor gets a SecureFault for a security error), and PERIPHACCERR is raised.

Each pin can be made secure in GPIOPORT[n].PERM, so that only secure code and secure peripherals can read or drive it; non-secure pins are open to both. If a non-secure peripheral's PSEL selects a secure pin, the selection does not take effect and the pin reads as zero; its other, non-secure pins are not affected. Pins handed to another domain through GPIO PIN_CNF[n].MCUSEL can be controlled and read only by that domain, under that domain's own security settings and PSEL registers; settings made by a domain that does not own the pin take effect only once MCUSEL gives it the pin. The application domain's GPIO registers stay writable under SPU rules while another domain owns a pin, but reach the pad only after MCUSEL returns the pin to the application domain.

Each DPPI channel can be made secure in DPPI[n].PERM, so that only secure peripherals can publish to it or subscribe to it. An event a non-secure peripheral publishes on a secure channel is ignored, and a non-secure peripheral subscribed to a secure channel receives nothing. No error is reported. The DPPIC is a split-security peripheral: non-secure accesses configure and control only non-secure channels, while secure accesses control all of them.

A channel group is non-secure if all its channels, enabled or not, are non-secure, and secure if any one is secure. Non-secure accesses to a register or bit field that controls a secure channel are ignored on write and read as zero, with no exception: for a secure channel i, non-secure writes to CHEN, CHENSET and CHENCLR cannot change bit i and reads give 0 there, and non-secure writes enabling or disabling group j (its TASK_CHG EN and DIS registers) are ignored when the group holds any secure channel. DPPIC.CHG[g] can be read or written by non-secure code only when all channels in it are non-secure. Group enable and disable tasks can be subscribed (SUBSCRIBE_CHG[n]) to channels of either kind; a secure group ignores events on non-secure channels, while events on secure channels reach groups of both kinds.
Other domains with their own CPU can reach the application core's peripherals, flash and RAM; SPU gives each such domain's transfers a security attribute through EXTDOMAIN[n].PERM.
Flash and RAM regions and the secure and non-secure peripherals each carry a TrustZone ID, distinct from the peripheral ID used to identify peripherals.
A set of interrupts is reserved for software use. The network core has four software interrupt instances, SWI0 to SWI3.

The temperature sensor measures the die temperature over a range at least as wide as the device's operating range, with 0.25 °C resolution; linearity compensation can be added if the application needs it. START begins one measurement; DATARDY marks its end and the result is read from TEMP, in 0.25 °C steps. The analog part powers down after each measurement, and every measurement needs its own START. The stated accuracy needs the crystal oscillator as HFCLK source. TEMP is a network core peripheral.

TIMER is a general-purpose timer/counter run from HFCLK, with a four-bit prescaler (division by 2^PRESCALER). It picks PCLK16M or PCLK1M by itself from the base frequency the prescaler sets, which is always 16 MHz divided by the prescaler: at fTIMER ≤ 1 MHz it uses PCLK1M to save power. Through PPI a TIMER event can trigger a task in another peripheral, and with GPIOTE it can make periodic outputs and PWM on any GPIO, as many as there are GPIOTE channels. START starts it and STOP stops it; START again resumes from the value it held. In timer mode the counter steps once per fTIMER tick; in counter mode it steps on each COUNT task, the prescaler is unused, and COUNT does nothing in timer mode. BITMODE sets the counter width and so its maximum; past the maximum it wraps to zero. CLEAR sets it to zero. PRESCALER and BITMODE must be changed only while the TIMER is stopped. Its accuracy is one fTIMER tick whatever the prescaler.

Each capture/compare register CC[n] has a CAPTURE[n] task that copies the counter into CC[n], and a COMPARE[n] event raised when the counter equals CC[n]; only the bits set by BITMODE take part in the comparison. With ONESHOTEN[n] set, COMPARE[n] fires once per write of CC[n], on the first match after that write.

Once the TIMER runs, CLEAR, COUNT and STOP take effect within one PCLK16M cycle. When START and STOP come in the same PCLK16M period, STOP wins. When CAPTURE and CLEAR come in the same PCLK16M period, CAPTURE wins, so CC holds the value from before the clear.

The TWI master with EasyDMA is a half-duplex two-wire master, I2C compatible, for several slaves on one bus, at 100, 250, 400 and 1000 kbps. It supports clock stretching by slaves (not I2C compliant: the SCL pulse after a stretched cycle may be shorter than I2C specifies). The bus is a bidirectional wired-AND pair, SCL and SDA, addressing up to 127 devices; TWIM is not CBUS compatible. SCL and SDA can each use any GPIO. TWIM works only as the single master on the bus; multi-master is not supported.

STARTTX or STARTRX starts TWIM and STOP stops it, followed by STOPPED. Once started, STARTTX or STARTRX should not be triggered again until LASTRX, LASTTX or STOPPED. SUSPEND (useful when the master is serviced from a low-priority interrupt) takes effect after the byte in progress and only during a transfer: TWIM raises SUSPENDED and stretches the clock until RESUME. It cannot be stopped while suspended, so STOP must follow RESUME. A NACK from the slave raises ERROR.
Peripherals with the same ID as TWIM share its registers, so all of them are disabled before TWIM is set up, and since disabling them resets nothing, every register in use must be written explicitly.
The pointer and count registers of both channels are double-buffered; the next transfer can be set up as soon as RXSTARTED or TXSTARTED is raised. STOPPED means EasyDMA has finished with RAM.

STARTTX sends a start condition, the address and a READ/WRITE bit of 0 (WRITE = 0, READ = 1); the slave answers with ACK (0) or NACK (1). After the ACK, TWIM sends the bytes from the buffer at TXD.PTR, each followed by an ACK/NACK from the slave. LASTTX is raised as the last byte starts. Neither the end of the buffer nor an error halts TWIM on its own:  STOP must be triggered during the last byte (the LASTTX_STOP short does this), from a PPI short, or from the error handler.

STARTRX sends a start condition, the address and a READ/WRITE bit of 1. After the slave's ACK, the slave sends data on TWIM's clock and the bytes go to RAM at RXD.PTR. TWIM ACKs every byte but the last, which it NACKs to end the read. LASTRX is raised when TWIM is ready for the last byte: after the ACK of the previous byte if RXD.MAXCNT > 1, or after the ACK following the address if RXD.MAXCNT = 1. STOP must be triggered before the NACK is due, at any time during the last byte; the LASTRX_STOP short is the recommended way. A full buffer or an error does not halt TWIM on its own either.

A write followed by a read (or a read followed by a write) with a repeated start is done with shorts: for example TXD.MAXCNT = 2 and RXD.MAXCNT = 4, STARTTX, LASTTX starting STARTRX, and LASTRX triggering STOP. When the driver runs in a low-priority interrupt and a more complex sequence is needed, SUSPEND and SUSPENDED keep the tasks in step, as in a double repeated start.
For the lowest current when TWIM is not needed, stop and disable it; after STOP wait for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE. STOP is not needed if TWIM is already stopped.

SCL and SDA go to the pins in PSEL.SCL and PSEL.SDA, which are written only while TWIM is disabled, used only while it is enabled and kept only in System ON; when disabled the pins act as ordinary GPIOs from OUT and PIN_CNF[n]. For correct levels in System OFF and while TWIM is disabled, the pins must be set up in GPIO as in the TWIM GPIO configuration. Only one peripheral may drive a pin.
The I2C specification limits line capacitance to 400 pF.

The TWI slave with EasyDMA is a half-duplex two-wire slave, I2C compatible, at 100 and 400 kbps, serving a single master on the bus. It can stretch the clock if the master supports that, and waits in a low power mode until it is addressed. PSEL.SCL, PSEL.SDA, CONFIG and ADDRESS[n] must be set before TWIS is enabled and changed only while it is disabled.

From IDLE, a read command with 'TX prepared' set takes TWIS to TX, which clears the flag and raises TXSTARTED; a write command with 'RX prepared' set takes it to RX, which clears that flag and raises RXSTARTED. A restart returns TX or RX to IDLE. A stop condition or the STOP task ends the transaction, clears both flags and raises STOPPED.
Peripherals with the same ID as TWIS share its registers, so all of them are disabled before TWIS is set up, and since disabling them resets nothing, every register in use must be written explicitly.

TWIS answers read and write commands only from IDLE, once enabled. It listens on up to two addresses, set in ADDRESS and enabled in CONFIG, and ACKs a read command (start, address, READ/WRITE = 1) only on a match, raising READ. If 'TX prepared' is set it enters TX at once; otherwise it stretches the clock until PREPARETX. In TX it sends bytes from the buffer at TXD.PTR on the master's clock, each followed by the master's ACK/NACK; the master NACKs the last byte it wants. At most TXD.MAXCNT bytes come from the buffer per transaction; further bytes are the ORC character and raise ERROR. The EasyDMA pointer and amount registers are captured when TXSTARTED is raised, and TXD.AMOUNT afterwards gives the bytes sent.

A write command (start, address, READ/WRITE = 0) is ACKed only on an address match and raises WRITE. With 'RX prepared' set TWIS enters RX at once; otherwise it stretches the clock until PREPARERX. In RX it ACKs every byte and stores it at RXD.PTR, up to RXD.MAXCNT bytes; extra bytes are NACKed and discarded and raise ERROR. The EasyDMA registers are latched at RXSTARTED, and RXD.AMOUNT afterwards gives the bytes received.

When the master writes, for example, two bytes and then reads four with a repeated start, and the slave learns what to send only from the bytes written, the READ_SUSPEND short holds the bus on the read command while the CPU handles the received bytes and prepares the reply (PREPARETX), and RESUME then continues.
If the master misbehaves, the STOP task ends the transaction: STOPPED is raised whether or not a stop condition appeared on the bus, and TWIS releases the bus and returns to IDLE.
For the lowest current when TWIS is not needed, stop and disable it; if STOP is sent, wait for STOPPED before clearing ENABLE.

SCL and SDA go to the pins in PSEL.SCL and PSEL.SDA, written only while TWIS is disabled, used only while it is enabled and kept only in System ON; when disabled the pins act as ordinary GPIOs. For correct levels in System OFF and while TWIS is disabled, the pins must be set up in GPIO as in the TWIS GPIO configuration. Only one peripheral may drive a pin.

The UARTE is a full-duplex asynchronous serial port with EasyDMA, up to 1 Mbps, with automatic hardware flow control (CTS, RTS), optional parity generation and checking, one or two stop bits, LSB first, and return to idle between transfers when flow control is used. Each signal can use any GPIO. The external crystal oscillator must be running for a clock accurate enough for reliable communication.

TXD.PTR and RXD.PTR must point into Data RAM, or an EasyDMA transfer may cause a HardFault or corrupt RAM. The pointer and count registers of both directions are double-buffered; the next transfer can be set up once RXSTARTED or TXSTARTED is raised. ENDRX and ENDTX mean EasyDMA has finished with the RX or TX buffer.

With the buffer at TXD.PTR and the byte count in TXD.MAXCNT, STARTTX starts sending. TXDRDY is raised after each byte, and ENDTX when all are sent, ending the transmission. STOPTX stops the transmitter and gives TXSTOPPED; ENDTX is raised on stopping if it has not been already. With flow control enabled (CONFIG.HWFC), sending pauses while CTS is inactive and resumes when it is active again; a byte already started is finished first. The transmitter uses least energy while stopped, before STARTTX or after STOPTX and TXSTOPPED.

STARTRX starts the receiver, which stores bytes by EasyDMA in the buffer at RXD.PTR (double-buffered, reloadable once RXSTARTED is raised) of RXD.MAXCNT bytes, raising ENDRX when it is full. RXDRDY is raised per byte, usually before the byte reaches RAM. RXD.AMOUNT after ENDRX gives the bytes written since the previous ENDRX. The ENDRX_STARTRX short restarts reception into the next buffer. STOPRX stops the receiver and gives RXTO; any pending ENDRX comes before RXTO, and none comes after it unless UARTE is restarted or FLUSHRX is used. If the buffer is not full when the receiver stops, ENDRX is still raised, before RXTO.

Up to four bytes can still arrive after STOPRX if the sender sends them right after RTS goes inactive. After RXTO the RX FIFO may still hold data; FLUSHRX moves it to RAM, after the buffer has been emptied or RXD.PTR moved so nothing is overwritten. RXD.MAXCNT must be greater than 4 to take the whole FIFO. ENDRX follows FLUSHRX even when the FIFO was empty or the buffer is not full, and RXD.AMOUNT then gives the bytes moved.

With flow control enabled, RTS goes inactive when the receiver is stopped by STOPRX or when the RX FIFO has room for only four more bytes. Without flow control the behaviour is the same but RTS is not driven, so no warning is given when four bytes of room remain, and data arriving with the FIFO full is lost; CTS and RTS are treated as always active. The receiver uses least energy while stopped, before STARTRX or after STOPRX and RXTO.

ERROR is raised for a framing error when a frame has no valid stop bit, and for a break when RXD is held low for longer than a frame; a framing error always comes before a break. ERROR does not stop reception: a byte with a parity error is still stored, followed by the bytes after it, while a byte with a framing error is not stored, though later bytes are.
CONFIG enables parity generation and checking for both directions (PARITY = Included), chooses even or odd parity (PARITYTYPE), and sets one or two stop bits (STOP).
For the lowest current when UARTE is not needed, stop and disable it; after STOPTX or STOPRX wait for TXSTOPPED or RXTO before clearing ENABLE. These tasks are not needed if UARTE is already stopped.

RXD, CTS (active low), RTS (active low) and TXD each go to the pin in their own PSEL register, written only while UARTE is disabled, used only while it is enabled and kept only in System ON. For correct levels in System OFF, the pins must be set up in GPIO as in the UARTE GPIO configuration. Only one peripheral may drive a pin.

The USB device controller is a full-speed (12 Mbps) device to USB 2.0, including the pull-up/pull-down resistors ECN and the 5 V short circuit withstand ECN, with the transceiver on chip and a D+ pull-up, also on chip, that software switches. It has 2 control endpoints (1 IN, 1 OUT), 14 bulk/interrupt endpoints (7 IN, 7 OUT) and 2 isochronous endpoints (1 IN, 1 OUT), double buffering on the isochronous endpoints, suspend, resume and remote wake-up, a 64-byte buffer per bulk/interrupt endpoint and up to 1023 bytes for isochronous endpoints, and EasyDMA for all data. It is an application core peripheral; a USB device stack is available in the Nordic SDK.

Software runs the USB 2.0 device state machine (attached, powered, default, address, configured, and suspended from each), driven by host traffic and bus states; USBDETECTED and USBREMOVED from the USB regulator report VBUS arriving and leaving. Host behaviour, including the order of commands during enumeration, should never be assumed: software reacts to the bus conditions and commands as they come.

For a full-speed device, D+ high with D- low is the J state and D+ low with D- high the K state. An idle bus, held only by the device's D+ pull-up and the host's pull-downs, sits in J. Both lines low is SE0 and both high is SE1.

D+ and D- are dedicated pins, not usable as GPIOs, and connect to the host. Under the 5 V short circuit withstand ECN they are not 5 V tolerant. They and the pull-up work only while VBUS is within its valid range and USBD is enabled.

The PHY is powered separately from VBUS and is switched with ENABLE; until its supply is up and stable the device cannot announce itself or handle traffic. USBD should be enabled only after VBUS is detected, and the pull-up turned on only after both USBPWRRDY and a USBEVENT with READY in EVENTCAUSE. A typical sequence: VBUS valid, USBDETECTED, ENABLE = Enabled and HFCLKSTART, USBEVENT with READY, USBPWRRDY, HFCLKSTARTED, then USBPULLUP = Enabled and enumeration begins. On VBUS removal (USBREMOVED), wait for EasyDMA transfers in progress to end (ENDEPIN[n], ENDISOIN, ENDEPOUT[n], ENDISOOUT) before disabling USBD; ENABLE reads Enabled until USBD is fully off.

The D+ pull-up tells the host a device is attached and that it is full speed. Without it the host's 15 kΩ pull-downs hold both lines low, the device is detached and may not draw VBUS current. Connecting the 1.5 kΩ pull-up attaches it; USBD supports only full speed and ignores high-speed negotiation. USBPULLUP connects or disconnects the pull-up, so software decides when enumeration happens and can emulate unplugging. It must be on for USBD to handle traffic and raise events, so an external pull-up cannot be used. Disconnecting it while attached lets the host pull both lines low and stops USBRESET from being raised. It is off after a chip reset and must be turned on only after USBD is enabled. Its value changes with bus activity per the resistor ECN, in hardware. DPDMDRIVE forces D+ and D- to the state in DPDMVALUE and DPDMNODRIVE releases them; this is not for normal traffic.

A USB reset is a bus condition, not a chip reset: SE0 lasting tUSB,DETRST, driven only by the host. USBD treats a longer SE0 as a USB reset and raises USBRESET; the USB stack and the parts of the application that depend on it then reinitialise and return to the default state. USBD disables all data endpoints and sets USBADDR to 0. After the pull-up is turned on the device ignores traffic until it has seen a USB reset, which USBD enforces. After a USB reset the device must be fully responsive within TRSTRCY of the USB specification.

The host keeps bus activity at least every millisecond; it suspends the device by leaving the bus idle in J. USBD detects inactivity longer than tUSB,SUSPEND and raises USBEVENT with SUSPEND in EVENTCAUSE; software must bring VBUS current within limits before T2SUSP and write LowPower to LOWPOWER to cut USBD's idle current. If nothing else needs it, the HFXO may be turned off during suspend, while the pull-up is disconnected, or with no VBUS; at all other times software must keep it on, as USBD cannot answer traffic without a stable HFXO.

When the host resumes (any non-J state) the device must answer within TRSMRCY and return to normal power; USBD raises USBEVENT with RESUME, or SOF events if the host just restarts frames. For remote wake-up, when supported and enabled by the host, software starts the HFXO, writes ForceNormal to LOWPOWER (which raises USBEVENT with USBWUALLOWED) and triggers DPDMDRIVE to drive a RESUME (K) state. DPDMVALUE = Resume leaves the duration to hardware (tUSB,DRIVEK); J or K holds that state until DPDMNODRIVE, and software must then meet TDRSMUP. DPDMVALUE is taken only when DPDMDRIVE is triggered. A wake-up must not be requested within TWTRSM after the bus goes idle; DPDMVALUE = Resume ensures this by delaying the RESUME state.

Each endpoint has its own registers, tasks and events, and endpoint 0 IN and OUT form the control endpoint. EPINEN and EPOUTEN enable endpoints. EPIN[n].PTR, EPOUT[n].PTR, ISOIN.PTR and ISOOUT.PTR give buffer addresses; EPIN[n].MAXCNT and ISOIN.MAXCNT the bytes to send next; EPOUT[n].MAXCNT (n = 1..7) and ISOOUT.MAXCNT the buffer length for incoming data, which can be copied from SIZE.EPOUT[n] or SIZE.ISOOUT since the host sets the size. EPOUT[0].MAXCNT is the control endpoint's OUT buffer length, and SIZE.EPOUT[0] reads the smaller of MaxPacketSize and the SETUP wLength. The AMOUNT registers give the bytes moved in the last transfer. EPSTALL stalls bulk/interrupt endpoints; hardware may override a stall on endpoint 0, for instance when a new SETUP arrives. SETUP data is not copied by EasyDMA but held in BMREQUESTTYPE, BREQUEST, WVALUEL/H, WINDEXL/H and WLENGTHL/H. EVENTCAUSE gives the cause of each USBEVENT, such as a CRC error or bus activity stopping or resuming.

The START tasks of each endpoint (STARTEPIN[n] and STARTEPOUT[n] for n = 0..7, and the two ISO ones) latch that endpoint's PTR and MAXCNT. On IN endpoints the USB transaction follows automatically once EasyDMA finishes; on OUT endpoints software allows the next transaction. On endpoint 0, EP0RCVOUT allows an OUT data stage, EP0STATUS starts the status stage and EP0STALL stalls the data or status stage. STARTED confirms capture of PTR and MAXCNT for the endpoints flagged in EPSTATUS, which may then be changed. ENDEPIN[n], ENDEPOUT[n], ENDISOIN and ENDISOOUT mean the whole buffer has been used and is safe to touch. Only one EasyDMA transfer can run in USBD at a time, so no START task may be triggered before the END event of the transfer in progress. EPDATA marks an acknowledged data transaction on the endpoints flagged in EPDATASTATUS, EP0DATADONE one on endpoint 0, and EP0SETUP a SETUP token with the setup data available in registers.

Endpoint 0 IN and OUT are the control endpoint, which every USB device must have. A control transfer has a setup stage, an optional data stage and a status stage, and is a control read, control read without data, control write or control write without data. EP0SETUP signals the setup data; data-stage bytes move by EasyDMA, and the control endpoint buffer can be any size. After a SETUP, USBD NAKs IN and OUT tokens until software has decoded the command and prepared the next stage. Software stalls an unsupported command, or one with bad wValue, wIndex or wLength, with EP0STALL. USBD handles SetAddress itself: software only updates its state machine and does not start a status stage; the assigned address can be read from USBADDR afterwards.

Software points EPIN[0] at the data and, with no other EasyDMA transfer running, triggers STARTEPIN0. STARTED (EPIN0 in EPSTATUS) means PTR and MAXCNT are captured and can be set for the next packet; ENDEPIN[0] means the data has left RAM; EP0DATADONE means the host has acknowledged it. Software repeats for more data or starts the status stage with EP0STATUS; the EP0DATADONE_EP0STATUS short does this when the data stage is a single transfer. With no data stage, EP0STATUS is triggered straight away.

Software points EPOUT[0] at the receive buffer and, with no other EasyDMA transfer running, triggers EP0RCVOUT so that USBD ACKs the first OUT+DATA. EP0DATADONE is raised as each OUT+DATA arrives, STARTED (EPOUT0 in EPSTATUS) when EPOUT[0].PTR and MAXCNT are captured, and ENDEPOUT[0] when the data is in RAM. Software then receives more by repeating, or starts the status stage with EP0STATUS; until then further OUT+DATA get NAK.

There are seven pairs of bulk/interrupt endpoints with fixed numbers. Each transaction is a single data stage; USBD toggles DATA0/DATA1 itself and holds the toggle when incoming data fails CRC so the host resends. DTOGGLE forces or resets the toggle of endpoint n (n = 1..7), as after ClearFeature, SetInterface or an alternate setting. A transaction is up to 64 bytes, and its buffer must be a multiple of four bytes, 32-bit aligned. After a completed IN transaction EPDATA is raised and IN tokens get NAK until new data has been moved (ENDEPIN[n]). Endpoints must be enabled in EPINEN or EPOUTEN to match the configuration chosen by SetConfig; a disabled endpoint ignores the host, an enabled one answers NAK, ACK or, if set in EPSTALL, STALL. HALTED.EPIN[n] and HALTED.EPOUT[n] read the halt state as a 16-bit value that can be returned as is for GetStatusEndpoint. Enabling or disabling an endpoint leaves its halt state alone; a USB reset disables all data endpoints and clears their halt. Endpoint 0 can be enabled and halted the same way, but a SETUP overrides its state.

operation.topic: USBD bulk and interrupt IN and OUT
operation.text: To send on an IN endpoint, software enables it (INn in EPINEN) and starts an EasyDMA transfer; an IN token can also be answered with a zero-length packet. Many hosts disable an interrupt endpoint that fails to answer three IN tokens, possibly needing re-enumeration, so data endpoints should be enabled as soon as SetConfig arrives. On an OUT endpoint the device NAKs until software writes any value to SIZE.EPOUT[n]; the next OUT+DATA is then ACKed and EPDATA raised (flagged in EPDATASTATUS). Writing EPOUT[n] and triggering STARTEPOUT[n] moves the data to RAM, and further OUT+DATA get NAK until ENDEPOUT[n] or until SIZE.EPOUT[n] is written again. The host may send zero-length packets.

An isochronous transaction is a single unacknowledged data stage following an IN or OUT token in each 1 ms frame. Software starts the EasyDMA transfers, in step with the SOF events. SOF timing is very accurate and SOF, synchronised to the 16 MHz clock, can drive PPI, for example to keep a local timer in step. Each SOF increments FRAMECNTR. ISO endpoints must be enabled in EPINEN or EPOUTEN; a disabled ISO IN endpoint does not answer and a disabled ISO OUT endpoint ignores traffic. A 1 kB internal ISO buffer goes wholly to IN or OUT, or is split between them with ISOSPLIT; the largest ISO transfer is 1023 bytes with the whole buffer and half that when split.

Enabled by ISOIN0 in EPINEN. After an EasyDMA transfer the endpoint answers the IN token with ISOIN.MAXCNT bytes; with no data moved, ISOINCONFIG.RESPONSE chooses no answer or a zero-length packet. A transfer not finished before the next SOF gives an undefined result. The buffer must be a multiple of 4 bytes, 32-bit aligned, but the packet can be any size up to 1023 bytes when the buffer is not shared with ISO OUT.

Enabled by ISOOUT0 in EPOUTEN. SIZE.ISOOUT gives the size of the last packet received. STARTISOOUT starts an EasyDMA transfer to ISOOUT.PTR of ISOOUT.MAXCNT bytes, kept in step with SOF (the SOF_STARTISOOUT short can trigger it). A transfer not finished before the next SOF gives an undefined result. The buffer in Data RAM must be a multiple of 4 bytes, 32-bit aligned; the packet can be up to 1023 bytes when not shared with ISO IN. A packet with a bad CRC raises USBEVENT (with SOF) and ISOOUTCRC in EVENTCAUSE, and EasyDMA still moves the data if set up.

Some registers cannot be reached while USBD is not enabled and ready (READY in EVENTCAUSE after a USBEVENT), or while it is in low power mode during suspend. This affects all tasks, PPI-triggered ones included, and these registers: the endpoint enables and stall (EPINEN, EPOUTEN, EPSTALL), the halt states (HALTED.EPIN[0..7], HALTED.EPOUT[0..7]), the setup data (BMREQUESTTYPE, BREQUEST, WVALUEL/H, WINDEXL/H, WLENGTHL/H), the OUT sizes (SIZE.EPOUT[0..7], SIZE.ISOOUT), and USBADDR, USBPULLUP, DTOGGLE, ISOSPLIT and FRAMECNTR.

The volatile memory controller powers the RAM blocks. Each block, which may hold several sections, can be powered up or down on its own in System ON and System OFF through the RAM[n] registers. In System OFF, RAM[n].POWER.RETENTION sets whether a section is retained; in System ON, the RETENTION and POWER fields set retention and access. Not retaining RAM lowers current consumption. The application core and the network core each have a VMC; the network core's has four RAM slaves.

The watchdog is a down-counter on LFCLK that guards against software lock-up. It is configured first and then started with START, which loads the counter from CRV; from then on CRV, RREN and CONFIG are locked. When the counter passes 0 it raises TIMEOUT. Starting it starts the 32.768 kHz RC oscillator if no other 32.768 kHz source is running. It can be set to pause while the CPU sleeps or is halted by the debugger; by default it keeps counting while the CPU sleeps. System OFF stops and disables it. The application core has WDT0 and WDT1 and the network core one WDT.
There are eight reload request registers RR[0..7], each enabled in RREN. Writing 0x6E524635 to every enabled RR reloads the counter from CRV.

TIMEOUT always leads to a watchdog reset. With the TIMEOUT interrupt enabled, the reset comes two 32.768 kHz cycles after TIMEOUT, and once TIMEOUT is raised the reset follows unless the watchdog is stopped. After any reset the configuration registers can be written again.

By default the watchdog cannot be stopped. To allow it, set CONFIG.STOPEN to Enable while configuring, write 0x6E524635 to TSEN, then trigger STOP; STOPPED is raised and CRV, RREN and CONFIG unlock. Writing zero to TSEN after the stop guards against runaway code triggering STOP.

The debug and trace system gives non-intrusive debugging. The application core's Cortex-M33 has an access port with eight breakpoints, four watchpoint comparators, ITM and ETM, and access protection by APPROTECT, ERASEPROTECT and SECUREAPPROTECT. The network core's Cortex-M33 has an access port with eight breakpoints, four watchpoints, and protection by APPROTECT and ERASEPROTECT. Debug uses Serial Wire Debug protocol version 2 with multidrop. A TPIU gives 4-bit parallel trace of ITM and ETM data (TRACECLK, TRACEDATA[0..3]) and serial wire output (SWO, on TRACEDATA[0]) trace of ITM data.

An external debugger reaches the device through a standard Arm CoreSight SW-DP using the two-pin SWD protocol on SWDCLK and SWDIO. SWDIO has an internal pull-up and SWDCLK an internal pull-down. The AHB-AP and APB-AP are standard Arm components; CTRL-AP is Nordic's own. TARGETID (DP register 0x4 with SELECT.DPBANKSEL = 0x2) identifies the target: designer code 0x144 (Nordic Semiconductor ASA) and part number 7 (nRF53 Series). DLPIDR (DP register 0x4 with DPBANKSEL = 0x3) gives protocol version 1 (SWD v2) and the target instance set by UICR.TINSTANCE.

The CTRL-APs are always reachable by a debugger; access to the system through each core's AHB-AP can be protected. On the application core, UICR.APPROTECT with CTRL-AP.APPROTECT.DISABLE controls the AHB-AP DBGEN signal, gating all non-secure access (readback protection of flash); UICR.SECUREAPPROTECT with CTRL-AP.SECUREAPPROTECT.DISABLE controls SPIDEN, which blocks secure access so only non-secure code can be debugged, and secure access needs APPROTECT open as well; UICR.ERASEPROTECT with CTRL-AP.ERASEPROTECT.DISABLE disables CTRL-AP.ERASEALL and NVMC ERASEALL, which with APPROTECT protects against readback and repurposing. On the network core, which has no TrustZone, UICR.APPROTECT with CTRL-AP.APPROTECT.DISABLE controls DBGEN, gating all AHB-AP access, and UICR.ERASEPROTECT disables ERASEALL.

For both cores the port is protected by default and opens only when UICR.APPROTECT is Unprotected and the CPU-side and debugger-side CTRL-AP.APPROTECT.DISABLE registers match; after reset the debugger-side value is known, so the CPU can open the port by writing it. The port is also open after a CTRL-AP.ERASEALL, which temporarily unprotects the AHB-AP until the next power-on, brown-out, watchdog or pin reset. So a protected device is unlocked by ERASEALL, programming firmware that writes UICR.APPROTECT = Unprotected, a reset, and the firmware writing CTRL-AP.APPROTECT.DISABLE. A debugger reads the protection state from the AHB-AP CSW register: DbgStatus shows whether AHB transfers are possible and SPIStatus whether secure ones are. When SPU grants the network core access to application core resources, the grant applies to the network core AHB-AP too.

Before using any access port the debugger requests power through CxxxPWRUPREQ in the SWJ-DP; while it does, the device is in debug interface mode, otherwise in normal mode. Current is higher in debug interface mode, so at the end of a session the debugger returns the device to normal mode and applies a pin reset. A few peripherals act differently in this mode. A power request while in System OFF wakes the device and sets the DIF flag in RESETREAS.

With breakpoints set in thread mode or in lower-priority interrupts, higher-priority interrupts still run to completion in real time, so code can be stepped without breaking real-time event-driven threads, such as servicing an external controller or sensor.

Each ROM table lists the CoreSight components on the debug port or AHB-AP so a debugger or on-chip software can find them. The application core ROM table at 0xE00FE000 points to the TPIU and to the Cortex-M33 ROM table at 0xE00FF000 (SCS, DWT, BPU, ITM, ETM, CTI). The network core's lists the Cortex-M33 ROM table with SCS, DWT, BPU and CTI; its ETM and ITM are not implemented.

A cross-trigger network starts and halts the cores together. Each core has a cross-trigger interface (CTI) that takes trigger inputs from the processor and debug blocks and routes them to trigger outputs, locally or over the cross-trigger matrix, which has four channels between the cores. To halt the network core whenever the application core halts, the application core CTI maps CTITRIGIN[0] (processor halted) to channel 0 with CTIINEN[0], and the network core CTI maps channel 0 to CTITRIGOUT[0] (debug request) with CTIOUTEN[0]. A fuller scheme carries application-to-network debug requests on channel 0, network-to-application ones on channel 1, and channel 2 for a common restart trigger from the debugger; each core sets CTICONTROL.GLBEN, routes its halted input to its own channel, and routes the other core's channel to DEBUGREQ and channel 2 to CPURESTART.

Multidrop SWD reaches any number of devices over one connection. To select this device the debugger writes TINSTANCE, TPARTNO and TDESIGNER, read from TARGETID and DLPIDR, into the SW-DP TARGETSEL register (Arm ADIv5.0 to ADIv5.2).

ETM and ITM trace leave through the 4-bit parallel TPIU (TRACEDATA[0..3], TRACECLK); the TPIU also offers serial trace over SWO. Parallel and serial trace cannot run together; ETM needs parallel mode, ITM works in both. The trace pins are dedicated pins shared with GPIOs, and SWO and TRACEDATA[0] use the same pin. TRACEPORTSPEED sets the speed, and the pins' speed also depends on the GPIO DRIVE setting in PIN_CNF[n]: only S0S1 (the reset default), H0H1 and E0E1 are for debugging, and H0H1, or E0E1 for the fastest speeds, is needed if the signals are too slow; software must not change it during the session. Each trace pin must also be given to trace and debug (TND) by PIN_CNF.MCUSEL, which makes it output-only and disables its other functions.

The sequence: enable the debug master (TAD ENABLE); request the clock (TAD CLOCKSTART); select the trace pins P0.08 to P0.12 in TAD PSEL.TRACECLK and PSEL.TRACEDATA0 to 3; give each trace pin to TND in its PIN_CNF with a high drive setting such as E0E1; set TRACEPORTSPEED, for example to 64 MHz; then configure the CoreSight components. Running the trace port below half the CPU frequency risks losing trace packets.

The control access port is Nordic's own access port for controlling the device when access port protection has shut the other ports. It offers soft reset, erase all, a mailbox, and debugging of protected devices. APPROTECT blocks the debugger from the AHB-AP and so from all CPU registers and memory-mapped addresses; it is set with UICR.APPROTECT and UICR.SECUREAPPROTECT together with CTRLAP.APPROTECT.DISABLE and CTRLAP.SECUREAPPROTECT.DISABLE, and the debugger can read its status. ERASEPROTECT protects flash and UICR from erasure and can be lifted temporarily from CTRL-AP. Its debugger registers are reachable only over SWD, not from the CPU; the SECUREAPPROTECT parts apply only to the core with TrustZone.
The debugger requests a soft reset through the CTRL-AP RESET register; firmware then sees the cause in RESETREAS.

Writing ERASEALL erases flash, UICR, RAM and all peripheral settings and lifts access port protection for a while; ERASEALLSTATUS reads busy meanwhile. At the end UICR.APPROTECT is set to Unprotected and both CPU-side DISABLE registers (APPROTECT and SECUREAPPROTECT) are set to 0x50FA50FA; after the next soft reset protection is off until a pin, power-on, brown-out or watchdog reset. An erase all aimed at the network core always erases the application core first, however it is protected. Writing UICR.ERASEPROTECT and resetting disables the CTRL-AP ERASEALL and leaves flash writes and erases to firmware, though the debugger can still write and erase while UICR.APPROTECT is not set; ERASEPROTECT does not affect debugger access. ERASEPROTECT.STATUS shows it.

A mailbox lets the CPU and a debugger exchange data over SWD: a TXDATA register with TXSTATUS and an RXDATA register with RXSTATUS on each side. When the sender writes TXDATA, hardware sets its TXSTATUS and the receiver's RXSTATUS to DataPending; when the receiver reads RXDATA, both return to NoDataPending.

With ERASEPROTECT enabled, the debugger and the firmware each write the same non-zero 32-bit key into their ERASEPROTECT.DISABLE registers; the device then erases itself as in erase all, returns to factory defaults and opens the access ports at the next reset. Firmware should set the write-once ERASEPROTECT.LOCK as early as it can, once it knows it needs no mailbox talk with a debugger; after that erase protection cannot be removed until reset.

Protection can be lifted temporarily for debugging. With UICR.APPROTECT enabled the port stays protected. Otherwise the debugger and the firmware write the same non-zero 32-bit key to the debugger-side and CPU-side CTRLAP.APPROTECT.DISABLE to open non-secure debug, and likewise to CTRLAP.SECUREAPPROTECT.DISABLE (with UICR.SECUREAPPROTECT not enabled) to open secure debug. The write-once APPROTECT.LOCK and SECUREAPPROTECT.LOCK should be set as early as possible in start-up; once written, that protection cannot be removed until reset. With secure debug open, an ERASEALL can also be started by writing the same key to both ERASEPROTECT.DISABLE registers. The DISABLE registers are reset only by pin, brown-out or watchdog reset, so a debug session survives soft resets. After ERASEALL the AHB-AP stays unprotected until a pin, power-on, brown-out or watchdog reset, so first firmware can be written. The AHB-AP CSW register's DbgStatus and SPIStatus fields show the state.
Each core has a CTI configuration interface at 0xE0042000: secure on the application core, non-secure on the network core.

TAD is the trace and debug control interface on the application core. Its trace PSEL registers exist, but for pin speed each trace function works on one fixed pin only, and writing any other pin number has no effect.

Most GPIOs can be routed to any peripheral, but four functions have pins of their own. 1 Mbps TWI: P1.02 and P1.03, chosen in the TWI PSEL registers, with E0E1 drive in PIN_CNF, which enables a 20 mA open-drain driver. QSPI: only P0.13 to P0.18, enabled by the Peripheral option of PIN_CNF[p].MCUSEL, with H0H1 drive. 32 Mbps SPIM4: P0.08 to P0.12, enabled by the Peripheral option of MCUSEL, which overrides the SPIM PSEL settings, with H0H1 drive. Trace: TRACEDATA[n] and TRACECLK with E0E1 drive and the TND option of MCUSEL. E0E1 drive exists only on P0.08 to P0.12 and on P1.02 and P1.03. High-speed signals need short PCB traces.
The aQFN94 has 94 pins plus four corner pads and an exposed die pad; the corner pads are not connected. The WLCSP has 95 balls.

Nordic recommends its own PCB layouts and component values for good RF performance; reference circuits exist for QKAA aQFN94 and CLAA WLCSP. VDD can supply external parts only when power comes in on VDDH. When USB is the only source, VBUS has to be tied to VDDH for USB to work. A regulator's DC/DC parts are needed only with its DC/DC mode on. NFC works in every configuration, and USB in every configuration where the host supplies VBUS. The optional series resistor on VBUS improves immunity to over-voltage transients when VBUS is plugged in.

In the reference layout for aQFN94 configuration 1, the RF capacitor C1 is not grounded straight to the ground plane: its ground runs through pin J31 to the VSS die pad, which adds filtering of harmonics. The layout uses four copper layers.

Every WLCSP variant reacts to visible and near infrared light, so the product has to shield the die, by its enclosure or by a shield or coating on the chip. CLAA has a light-absorbing film on the marking side; its edges and ball side are still exposed and need protecting.
